speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, I ask for the unanimous consent of the House to move a motion dealing with an important matter of pressing necessity.
Considering the alarming conditions of the French-speaking minority outside Quebec; considering the detailed report made by the association of that minority in its paper entitled: The Heirs of Lord Durham; considering that the government has remained silent following the cry of despair uttered by some 600,000 French Canadians outside Quebec who have already seen within a century 900,000 of their fellow-men irrevocably Anglicized; considering that the Prime Minister and other French-speaking ministers of Quebec ignore that small French-speaking minority to become concerned with the fate of an English-speaking minority in Quebec which is in no way threatened among 250 million English-speaking individuals, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier):
That the government undertake a detailed study of the conditions of Frenchspeaking Canadians outside Quebec to grant them, through the various provincial governments, the same rights and privileges given pursuant to Bill 1 under consideration at the Quebec National Assembly.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (Minister of Finance) moved
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE SUBSCRIPTION TO INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND AND INTERNATIONAL BANK FOR CONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
that Bill C-18, to amend the Bretton Woods Agreements Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.
Bretton Woods Agreements
He said: Mr. Speaker, the legislation before us today to amend the Bretton Woods Agreements Act aims to ratify the recently proposed amendments to the articles of agreement of the International Monetary Fund and to make them part of Canadian domestic law. The proposed amendments constitute the first major reform of the articles of the fund and represent a significant step in the evolution of the international monetary system. The bill also provides for acceptance of Canada's quota and subscription increases in the International Monetary Fund and the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development, or the World Bank. This is an important further step in the efforts which have been undertaken over the past six decades to try to work out in the international market an effective replacement for the role the gold standard played in monetary exchanges before the First World War.
Before that war was over, the first move in this direction was made with the publication of President Wilson's famous 14 points. At the Versailles conference which followed, an attempt was made to arrive at an international legal order which would govern economic relationships between states, but neither the treaties of Versailles nor of St. Germain-en-Laye were effective in bringing about the desired general improvement in the world monetary system. Indeed, the main feature of the interwar period with regard to international payments was, of course, the reparations question as it affected Germany, though in those decades the system was modified to some extent for instance, by the Dawes plan. With the worldwide depression in 1929, attempts to arrive at some collective world order in the economic field came virtually to an end and the period up to the beginning of the Second World War was one of economic autarchy.
After the conclusion of the Second World War there was, of course, an attempt-and a far more successful attempt-to create a number of institutions on the international scene for the purpose of establishing international economic order. There was a revival of the International Labour Organization, the only one of the League of Nations functional organizations which survived the war. Also, of course, there was the founding of the United Nations itself and the establishment of such specialist bodies as the World Health Organization and the Food and Agriculture Organization. The impetus with regard to a better world economic order was founded on the joint Anglo-American statement which emerged from the Atlantic Conference of 1941 between Prime Minister Churchill and President Roosevelt. At that time, the two leading countries on the western side in the Second World War sought to achieve a definition of multilateralism which would be useful in postwar reconstruction. The fourth and fifth paragraphs of the Atlantic Charter reflect this particular effort.
Out of that initiative, institutions such as the International Monetary Fund and the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development came into existence, as well as initiatives or the creation of the International Trade Organization, which was stillborn but which was followed by the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade. The two prime architects of the

May 24, 1977
Bretton Woods Agreements
Bretton Woods Agreement were the famous British economist, Maynard Keynes, and his American counterpart, Harry Dexter White. Richard Gardner, one of the leading students of this period, has written that the two men joined in their aim to promote a system of multilateral payments in which external equilibrium could be maintained at levels of domestic full employment. Their purpose was to provide members with additional international liquidity which would provide a protective cushion against temporary economic disturbances and make unnecessary the resort to illiberal internal or external policies.
The fund's articles of agreement have provided a legal and financial framework, just as the architects of the system had hoped, based on fixed exchange rates or par values, and these arrangements have continued to guide the international monetary system since the agreement was signed at the Bretton Woods conference in 1944. However, in recent years, particularly since the onset of the decade of the 1960s, it has become more and more evident that the par value system, as well as some operations of the fund, were no longer in tune with present-day international economic reality and with the needs of modern states. Canada in particular experienced difficulties in adhering to the rigid and anachronistic code. These difficulties led to the floating of the Canadian dollar in the 1950s and, again, since 1970.
As these problems surfaced, it became clear that the international monetary system as constituted by the articles of agreement, as well as the financial operations of the fund provided for by these articles, would have to be reformed and brought up to date. Thus, starting in the early 1970s the fund began to take a long and hard look at how such a fundamental reform might be achieved. A ministerial committee of 20 was created to seek a global reform of the monetary system. However, rapidly changing events such as the energy crisis and worldwide inflation made it impossible to achieve that aim. Accordingly, an evolutionary and more pragmatic approach to reform was adopted through the successor of C-20, the interim committee which, through much of its early years was chaired by my predecessor, the Hon. John Turner.
A reform package was finally agreed to at the interim committee's meeting in January, 1976, in Kingston, Jamaica, and this is the reform package which is now included in these amendments. Before the amended articles of agreement can come into effect, they must be ratified by 60 per cent of the fund's member countries with 80 per cent of the voting power.
These amendments to the Bretton Woods Agreements Act will, in addition, accept the increased quota of Canada in the fund, and increase it from special drawing rights $1,100 million to SDR $1,357 million as part of a general increase of subscriptions to the fund, from SDR $29 billion to SDR $39 billion which was proposed along with the amendments of the fund's articles. They represent, as well, an increase in Canada's subscription to the other Bretton Woods organization, the World Bank from U.S. current $1,136 billion to U.S. $1,342 billion. As only 10 per cent of our subscription to the World Bank is paid in cash, this will represent an out of pocket

contribution of about $20.6 million in Canadian dollars at this time.
The highlights of the new amendments are the new provisions on exchange rates which allow members to choose the arrangements which they wish to apply, the abolition of the official status for gold and the broadening of the scope of the IMF's surveillance powers to cover all policies that affect the external sector and not just exchange rate practices. In addition, some of the amendments improve the fund's operating structure and financial viability while others simply clarify the meaning or bring the wording up to date.
According to article I of its articles of agreement, the fund is charged with facilitating the expansion and growth of world trade and payments as a means of raising world standards of living and of fostering economic development. The fund is to promote and ensure stability and order with respect to exchange rates as well as to establish mechanisms for balance of payments assistance to enable member countries to correct temporary imbalances with a minimum of disturbance to the international monetary system. Accordingly, its assets are available for short and medium term financing to members faced with temporary balance of payments difficulties.
The general objectives of the fund are unchanged in the amended articles, although the means by which the fund and its members are meant to co-operate to achieve these objectives have been changed in key areas, particularly exchange rates, the role of gold and the financial operations of the fund. The fund's ability to enforce such co-operation with an international code of behaviour is based on its power to grant short and medium term credit under appropriate policy conditions to members.
Originally, the fund's membership consisted of 45 countries, as recognized in article II, section 1 and set out in schedule A of its articles of agreement. Provision was made in article II, section 2, for other countries to join, and currently its membership is made up of 128 countries, 100 of which are classified as developing countries. With the quota increase now proposed, total subscriptions to the fund through the years will have been increased to SDR $39 billion, which is about U.S. $45 billion at current rates of exchange, from original subscriptions totalling U.S. $8.8 billion; that is to say, in 1944 dollars. The bulk of its funds are obtained through quota subscriptions, although the IMF may borrow to help finance its operations.
The system as envisioned under the old articles required a member to declare and maintain a par value for its currency in terms of gold and to convert foreign official holdings of its currency into gold or the currency of the holder at the latter's request. When payments imbalances between countries produced a supply and demand situation that was not in balance at the existing exchange rates, governments intervened in the exchange markets to defend the par value. These interventions, in effect, financed the payments deficit or surplus. Although each country holds its own official reserves of gold and foreign exchange for this purpose, the members also draw upon the pool of other countries currencies in the fund.
May 24, 1977

The fund's financing operations take the form of a transaction. A member drawing on the fund uses its own currency to purchase foreign exchange from the IMF. It can purchase an amount equal to the gold part of its quota virtually automatically, and can purchase additional amounts, known as credit tranches, under progressively stronger policy conditionality and stiffer service charges. Borrowers must repay their loans by repurchasing their currency from the fund within three to five years.
This question of conditionality has been one of the questions that has excited considerable attention and concern at meetings of the interim committee. There is concern that the IMF bureaucracy in its application of the articles of agreement may fail to take account of the social and economic pressures which are weighing on the member countries, making applications for further balance of payments assistance under the fund. I, for one, share the concern which has been expressed by a number of ministers of finance in other countries that in the administration of its new powers the fund should seek on every occasion to remain sensitive to the difficult circumstances which member countries, and particularly developing member countries, are facing at present in an era in which there has been a dramatic increase in energy prices, and at the same time for some of the same countries a drop in export earnings. On the question of exchange rates, a new provision on exchange rates creates a general obligation for members to pursue policies conducive to a stable system of exchange rates.
Members must collaborate with the fund and with other members in this regard by pursuing domestic and external policies that are internationally responsible. Members are otherwise free to choose the exchange arrangements that best suit their circumstances. The fund has been given a new legal framework for the surveillance of the variety of exchange agreements that members adopt.
The exchange rate article also provides for a possible return to a par value system. If an 85 per cent majority in the fund believes it appropriate, the fund can enact a new system of fixed, but adjustable, exchange rates. However, the provisions clearly give a country the right to continue with any other exchange arrangement or to opt out of a reinstated par value system while still fulfilling the general obligations of good conduct. It is that exception which is of particular relevance from the standpoint of Canada, for Canada, as I have already said, is a country which, under the circumstances of our economy, has preferred to follow a floating exchange rate system.
There has been, in the international community, widespread experience with floating during the oil crisis, and the ability of the financial system to operate efficiently and viably in this atmosphere has helped support confidence in the arrangement. Canada was in the vanguard of the movement to float currencies and has naturally been a strong supporter of the swing back to greater flexibility, which is indicated by these amendments.
Bretlon Woods Agreements
The provisions of the new article on exchange rate arrangements is therefore very much in line with Canadian thinking and Canadian interests. As I have said, the amendment is fully satisfactory from the Canadian point of view. It gives the fund an appropriate role in monitoring financial practices, yet allows any government to pursue a responsible exchange rate policy suitable to its own circumstances. Necessary adjustments of exchange rates now have the potential of taking place swiftly and relatively smoothly, and thereby of absorbing the impact of payments deficits without forcing governments to intervene massively.
Among the important provisions in the amendment is a provision with regard to gold. The abandonment of par values, plus the problems of reserve creation and control, pointed to the need to phase out gold progressively from the monetary system. The provisions of the comprehensive amendment and the associated agreements on gold will greatly reduce the role of gold by removing its official status and allowing it to be traded like other commodities. The new articles eliminate the function of gold as a common denominator of par values. They abolish the official price and give members the authority to buy and sell gold at market prices. They eliminate all obligations on members to make payments of subscriptions, charges or re-purchases in gold to the fund. Thus, gold will no longer have a favoured role at the heart of the international monetary system, although it will still retain a monetary role for as long as nations hold it as part of their reserves. Through the new collaboration clause, members must undertake to ensure their policies with respect to reserve assets, including gold, better to serve international liquidity objectives. Finally, by an 85 per cent majority the fund may choose to dispose of its gold holdings.
As part of the agreement on these changes, the fund is to dispose of one-third of its gold holdings, half of this 50 million ounces being returned to members at the old official price of SDR 35 per ounce and half being sold on the market for the benefit of the least developed countries. So far, starting in June, 1976, the fund has held three auctions of its gold for the latter purpose. Profits from such gold sales will be used to assist the poorest developing countries meet their balance of payments needs. The fund has been pressed by Canada to make certain that the auctions are carried out with a minimum of disturbance to the regular production and sale of gold and with a minimum disruption to the market.
The reduction of the role of gold in the international monetary system has been in line with a position which Canada has consistently advocated, and the reduction of the role of gold seems to us a necessary step toward bringing liquidity creation under international control. We are satisfied that the arrangements in the new articles will lead toward this end.
In addition to those specific measures, the amendments now before the House contain quite a number of technical amendments with regard to detailed problems of application of the articles and in particular they confer upon the fund greater responsibilities with respect to the surveillance of balance of payments and other problems. On these matters I would be

May 24, 1977
Bretton Woods Agreements
more than happy to engage in a full examination and study with the committee when the bill receives second reading.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE SUBSCRIPTION TO INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND AND INTERNATIONAL BANK FOR CONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in speaking to this bill I must say that I find it remarkable that our minister has indicated how much the government endorses the amendments which are before us today with respect to changes in International Monetary Fund activities. For example, I believe the minister stated that the amendments-he was referring specifically to certain fixed rate exchange amendments-are fully acceptable to Canada. In short, without giving very many reasons as to why we should be asked to accept these amendments today, the government is obviously satisfied in its own mind that the amendments should be rubber-stamped and expedited through this House as quickly as possible.
While many of us may be overwhelmed by the subject matter before us today which is covered by Bill C-18-that is, amendments to the Bretton Woods Agreements Act-I suggest it is imperative that all hon. members of this House participate in a meaningful debate on this matter. In this connection I think it is regrettable that not one Liberal member chose to participate in the debate which dealt with the Customs Tariff revisions which were before the House last week. Not one Liberal member-other than the minister in each case-chose to join in the debate with respect to the excise tax amendments which were before this House, and I think it will be most regrettable if not one Liberal member chooses to speak on this bill which is before us today.
Surely hon. members opposite have some views as to what is the proper international monetary stance for Canada to be encouraging at the present time. Surely, if they are completely in agreement with the minister and with the other members of the cabinet, they could at least indicate to the House the nature of their agreement and why they feel we should be asked to support the amendments before us. There is little point talking domestically about how we intend to control inflation, how we intend to lessen unemployment, how we will ensure meaningful real growth in our economy, what is the proper fiscal and monetary stance for our country, whether the AIB is really needed, what course we should be following with respect to the GATT negotiations in Geneva, whether it is right for us to be borrowing so much exernally and, finally, why we have the trade deficit we have today in end products, for example, which has widened to a startling $10 billion, without first taking a good, hard look at Bill C-18 and its effect with respect to proposed amendments to the IMF.
There is little point debating these subjects unless we first debate what type of international monetary system we live with, how it should be changed to our advantage and, specifically, how any change in the international monetary system should be made to ensure that it is in Canada's best interests. Before we ask the nation to endorse these amendments, we owe it to our constituents to have a full debate first in this House and in committee with respect to the matters before us.

In leading off on behalf of the official opposition, I suggest there are ten points that we should be considering before we report this bill back from committee. First, since the establishment of the Bretton Woods Agreements 33 years ago, our international monetary system has attempted to free itself from any form of discipline. Unfortunately, Canada, both domestically and internationally, in the last ten years has been one of the most irresponsible partners in shedding such traditional constraints. As a result of this international lack of restraint, we find that the western industrialized world is being subjected currently to the highest interest rates since the middle ages. Let me reiterate that: I believe sometimes we grow accustomed to such things as 9, 10 or even 12 per cent interest rates without realizing that the phenomenon of high interest rates is truly an abnormal phenomenon and that we have not had, in the western civilized world, such high rates for the past 600 or 700 years. That is the first point I wish to make. Historically there is very little doubt that the fall of interest rates such as occurred in the western world from the thirteenth century onward reflected a healthy growth in our civilization and denoted a real growth for all concerned. I would point out that there are a number of phases where interest rates have gone up-not to the present height, but higher than normal. This has always been associated with unstable political and economic conditions. Likewise, rises in interest rates denote a civilization in trouble as occurred in Roman times and earlier. With interest rates, particularly in Canada, at such record heights, somewhere in the 9 per cent range, I think it is important that we compare that 9 or 10 per cent range with the 4 per cent range of interest rates in the world's nine strongest nations, Canada included, over the past 200 years. I believe we should accept such high interest charges as a red flag indicating danger, certainly for this country and, secondly, for the western industrialized world.
Second, in our participation with respect to the International Monetary Fund the impression has been left that in Canada we do not have an independent mind. I believe the speech of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) today brings this out most vividly. There is no questioning; everything is acceptable that has been put before us as far as the proposed amendments are concerned. There is no uncertainty in the minister's mind about whether the amendments before us are totally acceptable to Canada. He does not give the pros or cons. In short, it appears that we have simply followed the lead of the United States: if it is good for the United States, the assumption is that it is good for Canada. This is unfortunate, in that in dealing with this matter there is no doubt that the interest and objectives of the United States are often quite different from ours. It is true, we share this great continent together, but this does not mean that automatically what the United States wishes to change with respect to the International Monetary Fund is necessarily good for us.
We should remember, for example, that the United States is one of the most efficient producers in the world. It is, therefore, natural, being such good producers, that they want an
May 24, 1977

open world so that they can sell their produce. This, if allowed to happen, and coupled with the equal production efficiency of Japan and Germany, would devastate this country as a manufacturing nation. This trend is reflected in the economic review tabled by the Minister of Finance last week, where it is pointed out on page 60 that our trade deficit in end products rose from $3.6 billion in 1971 to over $10 billion-the figure I referred to earlier-in 1975 and 1976. In sharp contrast, the United States, Germany and Japan had surpluses in their comparable and product accounts.
Third, the government has chosen a policy of relative secrecy with respect to negotiations which have led to the amendments before us. Unfortunately, they have chosen to be secret about our GATT negotiations in Geneva as well. This shroud of secrecy surrounding government activities is contributing to the lack of business confidence so prevalent today. How can we expect labour, small businessmen and farmers to co-operate if we do not take them into our confidence with respect to the government's targets and objectives? Only last Friday we had an example of the government's tendency to be non-committal with respect to our future or the future the government hopes to chart for us. When asked during the question period if the government would follow the lead of President Carter's chief economic adviser, Mr. Charles Shultz, and announce a target date for bringing the Canadian budget into balance, the Minister of Finance only stated that he admired the courage showed by Mr. Shultz but he, himself, did not care to be so precise.
For years the Americans have published their long-term objectives with respect to inflation, unemployment, interest rates and the like, while our government officials merely dodge the issue, leaving the impression that the Americans know where they want to go and what they want to achieve, while our officials are totally bewildered.
Fourth, this government likes to cite the energy pricing crisis as being troublesome in Canada. It is true that the oil producing countries as a whole had current account surpluses of about $46 billion in 1976. But today and earlier it is interesting to note that the Minister of Finance forgot to point out that we are an energy producing nation and that every year since the so-called crisis in pricing we have produced a trade surplus in energy by selling at high prices. Last year, for example, our surplus was about half a billion dollars on energy trade alone. How strange that we are constantly told that energy pricing is creating domestic problems in Canada, when in fact we are the beneficiaries, as far as trade is concerned, in high-priced energy that is being sold throughout the world.
I suggest that energy pricing has a minimum effect as far as trade is concerned, that is, whether we are doing well or poorly in terms of world trade rather than ending up as we did in 1975 with the highest current account trade deficit of any of the seven major industrial nations; and then rationalizing the situation. It is time government supporter recognized the degree of severity of that deficit. Canada, in short, had the highest current account trade deficit of any of the seven major industrial nations, including the United States, Japan, France,
Bretton Woods Agreements
Germany, Italy, the United Kingdom and ourselves. In 1976 we were the second highest in our deficit, trailing only France.
Fifth, I would like to suggest that the world's real growth expansion in the past few hundred years has been subjected to monetary discipline. First it was gold that was the agreed standard, but as it shackled those who wished to spend, it was downgraded until now, in the amendments before us today, gold has been downgraded to virtually no role. Let us face the fact that the chief reason those who are proposing our present monetary system have discarded and downgraded gold is that they do not like to be disciplined by the effect gold has when our monetary system is related to it. I noticed that in his earlier remarks the Minister of Finance, in effect, endorsed the downgrading of gold as far as our international monetary system is concerned. As the world's third largest producer of gold, are we right in accepting this relative abandonment of a world standard that has been with us throughout history?
The more the world depends on the United States dollar and the use of the SDR, the more the world leaves itself open to the irresponsible expansion of money. The amendments to the Bretton Woods Agreements being debated today will in many ways leave the world's monetary system open to domination by the United States monetary approach. If the United States inflates, the world will tend to inflate. If the United States
restrains,	the world will tend to be restrained. In short, international monetary leaders can print money, but they have not learned how to produce gold, which is why recourse to gold is resisted.
We in Canada must ask ourselves if this system best suits our interests. Is the complete abandonment of gold in Canada's best interests? It is not that gold is so important. Its importance, rather, is that its use involves a built-in element of
restraint.	One asks, given the new, liberalized use of SDRs and other forms of international currency, what will impose a tolerable degree of restraint on governments? Given the opportunity, most governments will sidestep restraint, as our own government has. You will recall that it doubled this country's money supply in the six-year period ending last October because it found that course politically beneficial.
Sixth, while we have been referring to the structuring of the international monetary system and to the fact that world leaders appear to be seeking relative freedom to "gimmick" the monetary system at will, I suggest it is important for the government to indicate to the House how it plans to act responsibly in the midst of possible world irresponsibility. By being restrained in this country, by running our own system prudently, we can turn international irresponsibility to our advantage, as Switzerland has done, for example. Swiss currency has appreciated in relation to other major currencies, while ours has depreciated. In short, to the degree other nations choose to create inflation domestically, we in Canada can improve our position by deliberately containing inflation which, in turn, will be of benefit to us internationally.

May 24J977
Bretton Woods Agreements
It is absolutely erroneous to say that a nation must inherit inflation created outside its boundaries. The fact is that Canadian inflation was manufactured by the Bank of Canada under the instructions of the Canadian government. There is no doubt about it, although the government likes to confuse the issue. Such inflation need not be imported. Actually, it will only be imported by a government which chooses to avoid fiscal and monetary responsibility, as the minister well knows.
Let me put it this way: If the minister goes to the local pub and sees some people who have drunk too much and are, therefore, in a state of drunkenness, that does not mean that he, himself, must get drunk. But that is the idea he wants us to accept when he talks about world inflation, or inflation in other nations. When the minister speaks of inflation, which is only another form of a binge at the local world pub, the minister likes to pretend that if other countries are giddy, we, somehow, must become giddy too. That is not true. Unfortunately, the minister has not said today what steps he intends to take to make sure that despite any inflationary tendencies which may develop internationally we shall curb inflation in this country.
Seventh, not only has Canada tended to acquiesce in the world's credit explosion, but we have reached the peak in foreign borrowings. I wish to read three passages from the Economic Review to which I have referred. The parts 1 shall quote are relevant to Canada's present-day position in the international world. The first passage reads:
The substantial increase in Canada's current account deficit has been matched by an increase in net over-all capital inflows, particularly through an increase in new issues of long-term Canadian securities abroad. This resulted in a rise in the book value of Canada's balance of international indebtedness (including increases in earnings accruing to non-residents) from $29 billion at the end of 1971 to $48.5 billion at the end of 1976.
Mr. Speaker, to sum up, according to the minister's own economic review figures our total foreign debt increased by almost $20 billion between 1971 and 1976 over the previous $29 billion level. It took Canada 104 years to run up a foreign debt of $29 billion, but in five years-between 1971 and 1976-the government, through sheer irresponsibility, increased that foreign debt by $20 billion. I continue quoting the first passage:
As noted earlier.. . the increase in indebtedness has caused interest payments to non-residents to increase at a rapid-pace during the past five years, thereby making turn-around in the current account more difficult to achieve.
The second passage I wish to quote reads as follows:
The net capital inflow of $4.9 billion in 1976 was marginally higher than in the previous year, reflecting a steep rise in long-term capital inflows and an off-setting decline in the balance on short-term capital. The net long-term inflow of $7.5 billion was up $3.4 billion from the previous year-
To summarize, that passage refers to the inflow of long-term capital, capital which will not be repaid for 5, 10, 15 or more years. Such capital inflows of $7.5 billion last year increased by $3.4 billion over the level of the previous year. The final paragraph I wish to quote reads in part:
-net new issues placed abroad, including both foreign currency and Canadian dollar issues, accounted for 60 per cent of all net new marketable issues by Canadian borrowers, compared with 45 per cent in 1975.

I emphasize that these are not our own figures or the figures of some outside group. They represent the government's own admission of the extent of this country's foreign borrowings. The impact of this borrowing binge will be felt for generations in Canada. It will be felt in particular as the money has been substantially used to finance consumer purchases rather than capital projects which might have been used to improve our international trading position in years to come.
As we know from Canadian history, initially we borrowed large sums from Great Britain and certain other nations. But we did not borrow to cover current account trade deficits, which is now the case. We borrowed money to build our railways and to build power installations which in turn helped develop our country. The prosperity which resulted gave us the wherewithal to pay back the debt. That is not happening now. We are not doing this with respect to the debt we are now incurring internationally.
Eighth, the drift to non-fixed exchange rates has been encouraged or at least supported by the International Monetary Fund, as the minister said today. We in Canada have been in the vanguard in asking for free exchange rates as opposed to the traditional fixed approach. This, coupled with our tendency to borrow so extensively to cover our inadequate trade position, leads to interest rate crunches. Already we have had our first run on the Canadian dollar. Hon. members will recall last November. We were lucky. The minister covered up and we were sheltered from the true impact as to what actually occurred in November and December of last year. Here, again, the Economic Review discloses that in November of that year our United States dollar reserves fell by $758 million. That, Mr. Speaker, is a tremendous fall for our reserves in any one month, bearing in mind that our total reserves are less than $4 billion. The review points out that the rise in December was roughly comparable to the decline in November. They state at page 65:
The Canadian dollar was under heavy downward pressure in November but recovered in December.
When we get to committee, I hope we can be furnished with sufficient information so that the Canadian public will be fully apprised of exactly what happened in November and December during that mini-crisis. If we can get that information we may be better prepared for future runs on the Canadian dollar which will certainly occur if the Canadian government persists in their "Alice in Wonderland" approach to international finances. With our resources, which on a per capita basis are greater than the resources of our rival industrialized nations, it is inconceivable that we should some day have to be bailed out by the International Monetary Fund like the United Kingdom has been. However, that is certainly what will happen if we continue on our present path.
Ninth, the minister has not given us today, and certainly has not earlier given any indication whether the International Monetary Fund or any other international agency has given guidelines to this nation or any other nation which are to be
May 24, 1977

followed domestically by member countries with respect to monetary increases. In Canada the increase in our monetary aggregates went on virtually unabated in 1975 and 1976 when, we are told, we were in a period of so-called restraint.
Here are the facts: M-2, which is currency and privately-held Canadian deposits, jumped 17.5 per cent in 1975 and 17 per cent in 1976. With such expansion, and with our rapid expansion in the government sector, the Anti-Inflation Board activities have become an exercise in futility. Worse still, the AIB appears simply to be a convenient scapegoat to allow the government to pretend to the Canadian public that they are doing something meaningful about inflation.
Surely we are entitled to get from the minister some indication as to whether such monetary increases are within, or without, suggested word guidelines. Is it in the current thinking of the International Monetary Fund, for example, that a country such as Canada should expand its most basic supply of money by approximately 17 per cent in a year? Is it really being fair to the Canadian public, with such expansion, to be stating that somehow restraint is the order of the day?
The tenth point I would like to make is that while we have already cited Canada's high interest structure, perhaps the most ludicrous thing of all is that we, a high-interest rate country, is in the vanguard of making low-interest loans directly or indirectly throughout the world. In the World Bank annual report for 1976, which of course includes funds from this country, billions of dollars are listed as going out to various countries or organizations at interest rates substantially below the rates that we must pay when Canadian identities borrow abroad. In appendix H to the World Bank annual report for 1976 records are shown for hundreds of countries. The loans I would like to refer to are those listed for the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development which, of course, is a World Bank, International Monetary Fund activity. They indicate that the current rates in the year under review were 4.5 per cent to 8.85 per cent. The countries they list include, for example, Bolivia, Chile, the Congo, Fiji, Peru and Turkey. Virtually any country that you want to think of is listed as getting loans in the range of 4.5 per cent to just slightly under 9 per cent.
Perhaps the minister can explain how we have gotten into a system where such countries are entitled to credit at those rates when, at the behest of the federal government, our provinces have to borrow abroad at interest rates of 9, 10, and even 11 per cent. Perhaps the minister can also explain why, in this international context, our Export Development Corporation makes loans amounting to hundreds of millions of dollars with interest in the 8 per cent range, yet we are told there are no funds available to allow the government to meet their election promise of supplying $290 million to help urban transit in Canada. Why the double standard?
With one of the highest interest rate structures of any of the industrialized nations, why do we feel there is nothing inconsistent about giving loans with interest rates substantially below the rates we are requiring Canadians to pay domestically?
Bret ton Woods Agreements
It is perhaps axiomatic that the needs of international commerce change more rapidly than our ability to cope with them. In the past few years, for example, we have seen massive and, as I have said, disproportionate shifts of wealth away from the industrialized nations and into the coffers of the oil exporting nations. As I have already mentioned, let us not forget that we are an oil exporting nation.
It is estimated that in 1976 the OPEC countries may have sustained a combined surplus as high as $46 billion, while the OECD nations stumbled along with a current account deficit of $20 billion. May I again remind hon. members that of that $20 billion sustained by OECD countries, over 20 per cent is Canada's deficit, that being the $4.3 billion that we ran up in our current account trade deficit last year. It is within this context of a rapidly changing world order that the amendments to the Bretton Woods Agreements were drafted. It is within this context that we, in dealing with Bill C-18, must attempt to determine just where the world is heading today and where Canada will fit into any new order.
There is growing concern that our international monetary system is faltering today and that increased flexibility in exchange rates may be partly at fault. If I judged his remarks correctly, the minister almost takes credit for the relative free floating of exchange rates in the world. I would point out to him that Dr. F. Leutwiler, president of the board and general manager of the Swiss National Bank, had this to say about the current state of international monetary conditions:
The breakdown of the formerly stable monetary system was not caused by inadequate rules as may perhaps be presumed, but eventually by the inability to live up to the disciplinary constraints of the parity system . ..
It is therefore in no way surprising that the monetary reserves of the western world increased in 1974 by no less than $37 billion; at the end of 1975 they amounted to a total of $230 billion. This is roughly 2'h times as much as in 1970.
Let me repeat, that, Mr. Speaker-by 1975 international monetary reserves went up 214 times what they were in 1970. To continue with Dr. Leutwiler's quotation, he states:
Thus, apart from inflationary domestic money creation as a seemingly easy means of evading the constraints of stability policy, international money creation-no less inflationary-was also practised.
He concludes:
It is obvious that deficit financing via borrowings is not practicable over a prolonged period of time.
Theoretically, Mr. Speaker, there are many advantages to flexible exchange rates. They dispense with the necessity of keeping large exchange reserves. They allow changes to take place gradually and they make speculation more difficult. But that is theory, Mr. Speaker. In practice, many of these advantages fail to materialize. We have had rather violent changes in a number of currencies, such as the lira and the pound, and there is a danger that a growing number of weak currencies, our own potentially included, may have further crisis periods to go through.
A greater flexibility in our current system of floating exchange rates has not led to the gradual lifting of controls, as many had hoped. Rather, it may have contributed to the

May 24, 1977
Bretton Woods Agreements
breaking up of the world into currency blocs. Economists such as France's Michel Lutfulla envision four evolving currency blocs: the United States dollar zone, the Japanese yen zone, the European snake centred around the Deutschmark, and possibly an Arab oil-producing bloc. Rather than facilitate the expansion of worldwide trade and investment, these blocs may indeed herald an age of trade within, rather than between, the major zones. The implications for Canada are surely obvious. Where will we belong? Will we be aligned to the United States currency bloc, largely as a result of our substantial trade with that country, or are we to develop the so-called third option and align ourselves to Europe and Japan?
There is also growing concern in many quarters over the ability of the International Monetary Fund to meet the tremendous demands that are made on it. The United Kingdom recently received $3.9 billion from the IMF. Mexico, too, negotiated a loan of nearly $1 billion, causing many analysts to speculate on whether the IMF has enough reserves to cover even these loans, much less meet the demands of the future. Will Canada be called upon to make increasing commitments to the fund? I suggest that this is something we must explore more fully in committee. On this point we must ask ourselves to what extent, and to what lengths, we are prepared to bail out other countries. Hon. members should bear in mind that fluctuating currencies and supernational currencies, such as SDRs, lend themselves quite handily to camouflaging the true cost of foreign assistance.
It will be especially difficult for us to determine the extent to which our so-called aid to the companion bill to Bill C-18, Bill C-5, would remove from parliamentary scrutiny the Auditor General's report on the foreign exchange account. You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that that bill that is C-5 contemplates that that report will now go to the Minister of Finance, as opposed to the parliament of Canada.
Even if we can determine the extent of our assistance, the question remains, how far should we go? Does it make any sense, for example, that we borrowed abroad, as I have indicated, in 1976 at record levels and at record interest rates, and we then turn around and lend $300 million to Peru at greatly reduced rates? The World Bank annual report to which I have referred states that in the first half of 1976 Canada borrowed abroad $5.3 billion, fully 42 per cent of that taken down by all the world industrialized nations combined. Let me re-emphasize that. According to the World Bank, in the first six months of 1976 Canada's borrowing was 42 per cent of all the world's external borrowings combined. We borrowed Vk times the amount borrowed by the second largest borrower, France, and more than Austria, Belgium, Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, Iceland, Ireland, Italy, Liechtenstein, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Norway, Sweden, Switzerland, the United Kingdom and all the multinational corporations combined. We borrowed nearly 29 times the amount borrowed by the United States in the first half of 1976.
Those figures are to be found in the World Bank report to which I have referred. Last year, Canadians took down more than $8 billion abroad in long-term debt alone. At an average

rate of 9 per cent, we added to our national service charge more than $700 million. This is in addition to our total foreign indebtedness, which in 1975 totalled $43 billion. The service payment on this amount alone costs Canadians about $2 billion, according to recent estimates made by the C.D. Howe Institute. This is a record for Canada, and possibly even for the world, as we accounted for approximately 20 per cent of all new international bond issues in medium-term Eurocurrency credits last year. This year it is estimated that our borrowing will be down to perhaps $4.5 billion or $5 billion, but based on current increases in foreign debt costs, Canadian exporters must increase their trade surpluses by about $500 million each year just to keep our over-all current account deficits from getting worse.
Here we are caught in a vicious dilemma. We have been mortgaging our future at such an alarming rate that we are getting to the point where there is no easy way to extricate ourselves. The competitive ability of our Canadian manufacturing industries, already reeling from high labour costs, low productivity and other disadvantages, can hardly afford the added penalty of a Canadian dollar kept artificially high due to such large influxes of foreign capital. Yet if our dollar were to depreciate by any substantial amount, our soaring foreign debt costs would increase all the more, making it that much harder to reverse the large current account deficits of recent years. In fact, one official of the C.D. Howe Institute has warned that if we were to continue borrowing at recent levels we would eventually be facing such bad balance of payments problems that the IMF would have to become involved in Canada, as I have already said.
In dealing with this general subject, Mr. Speaker, I think all members would be interested in a speech given by J. Anthony Boeckh at the Financial Analysts Federation annual conference held May 1 to 4 of this year. Mr. Boeckh listed for the conference five symptoms of what he called a "secular malaise". The first was price inflation; the second, public sector deficits; the third, balance of payments deficits and weak currencies; the fourth, foreign debt; and finally, high interest rates. Those were the five headings set out by Mr. Boeckh, and I suggest that we have inherited all five problems in Canada. On the subject of price inflation, Mr. Boeckh had this to say:
It is now over three years since the big OPEC oil price rise and the peak in global money and price inflation occurred, yet only Germany, Switzerland and the U.S. have brought price-inflation down to 5 per cent or less... In countries such as Canada the inflation has been held to around 8 per cent only by wage-price controls and an overvalued currency.
On the subject of public sector deficits, Mr. Boeckh stated that public sector borrowing as a percentage of the gross national product is currently around 8 per cent in Canada, in contrast to Germany where it is about 4 per cent, and the United States and Japan where it is about 3 per cent or less. Dealing with balance of payments deficits and weak currencies, he said that a third common characteristic of those countries in the most serious trouble is massive balance of payments deficits. If the currency of a financially troubled country is supported by restrictive monetary policy and high
May 24, 1977

interest rates, as in Canada's case, unemployment must rise and the balance of payments remain huge. Dealing with foreign debt Mr. Boeckh stated that a fourth characteristic of the malaise is a progressive reliance on foreign debt to finance balance of payments deficits, and from an internal point of view, to finance excessive consumption both private and public. Mr. Boeckh also stated that Canada is, again, a classic example, having borrowed some $9 billion abroad last year to finance a $5 billion current account deficit as well as major capital outflows.
Our capacity for further borrowing is in serious question. The experience of Italy and the United Kingdom is a classic example of countries which borrow massively abroad. Such is the fate of all countries which borrow to finance excessive public and private consumption at home, as opposed to borrowing to build plant and equipment and finance other investments which produce things which can be sold and which have a rate of return sufficiently high to provide funds to eventually liquidate the foreign borrowings that originally took place. Those countries which continue to run large budget deficits, balance of payment deficits, and borrow heavily abroad to finance them, must at some point suffer a major domestic financial crisis. I emphasize that I am again quoting Mr. Boeckh.
Finally, dealing with interest rates, Mr. Boeckh stated that for a country suffering the symptoms I have mentioned, high interest rates are an inevitability: they are essential to restrain liquidity, to finance large balance of payments deficits and to prevent currency depreciation. Countries that have inflated heavily must necessarily have very low levels of liquidity and very high inflation premiums built into the level of interest rates. One can virtually rate the financial and economic health of nations by the level of their interest rates. He compared corporate bond rates in Italy, the United Kingdom, France, and Canada, with Switzerland, Germany, Japan and the United States. In truth, the discrepancy is most remarkable. Generally speaking, the intensity of the symptoms roughly corresponds to the rate of growth of the public sector relative to the private sector. As government spending, transfer payments and subsidies to the public sector and to private corporations expand, there must necessarily be a structural crowding-out of the private sector which actually produces goods and services that can be sold.
Mr. Speaker, this is the point. We are not suggesting that we should, in any way, ignore our responsibilities abroad, nor are we advocating that we shrink from our real responsibilities as good international citizens. We are merely suggesting, in order to be good world citizens, that we must first put our own financial house in order. As one British banker told the conference board recently, one would emphasize to those responsible, within their capacities as national statesmen and officials for domestic finance, that the instability in the international relationship of currencies reflects the depreciation at different rates of the internal value of those currencies.
Bretton Woods Agreements
The more they are able to do to control inflation at home, the easier it will be to devise and operate an international system not subject to periodic crises. More flexible or fluctuating rates of exchange should not, above all, be considered as a soft option to governments wishing to avoid balance of payments constraints respecting the adoption of inflationary policies. In other words, we cannot rely on the world to bail us out if we mismanage at home.
There is a growing need for the reintroduction of self-discipline in our international monetary order. As the demand for fair international liquidity has increased in the post-war period, the more inelastic features of the Bretton Woods Agreements have fallen by the wayside. Self-regulation maintained a reasonable equilibrium in the system until about 1966 when Great Britain and the United States, under the Kennedy influence, began to introduce, bit by bit, irresponsibility into the international system. Today, 10 or 11 years later, the system is so precarious that we find one central bank rationalizing for another what is, in truth, irresponsible behaviour.
We have witnessed the ludicrous spectacle of officials laying the blame for domestic ills in other more international corners than their own-and none does this more than this Trudeau government. We are now paying the bill for such short-sightedness. In the early 1970s there was an almost universal stimuation of the world economy which, together with the attempt to maintain 1971 exchange rates, led to the rapid inflation of 1972-74. On the other hand, West Germany and Switzerland resisted the global temptation, and today remain relatively sound.
History teaches us much, but it also teaches us that we cannot necessarily know what is coming in the future. The course of the International Monetary Fund is uncertain, and in the years ahead it may be even more troubling with the mounting debt of the Third World. Other colleagues of mine will be speaking about the mounting debt of the Third World. That is why we are proposing to take an overview of our economic relationship with the world. We hope, in committee, to take a good, sober look at the future.
I would like to close by simply referring to history, and in particular to a history of interest rates written in a rather monumental report by Sidney Homer in 1963. He was a New York financial house executive who had kept track of interest rates throughout the world since 2000 years before Christ. He stated that the health of a country can virtually be identified by the level of interest rates. He pointed out that a study of nine European and North American countries over the past two centuries clearly demonstrates that relationship.
Amongst those commercial nations, long-term yields have tended to be low or lowest in those countries which have been politically, commercially and financially the strongest. I would like to conclude by simply saying: Let us take heed. If we feel we have certain instability in this country at the present time, and if we feel we have certain groups who are advocating separatism, let us bear in mind the fertile ground through the insecurity of wrong financial management has been laid by

May 24, 1977
Bretton Woods Agreements
this government in Ottawa, and unfortunately we in Canada must now reap the whirlwind.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE SUBSCRIPTION TO INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND AND INTERNATIONAL BANK FOR CONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened with great pleasure over the years to the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens), and I have always known that sooner or later he would blow a fuse in the House of Commons. He managed to do that today. We have had this little light trickling down in the course of a great intervention. We have three official languages in the House of Commons. We have French and English, of course, but we have a language called "hustings". I think we were subjected to that language, on both sides, today.
I would like to start with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) because I tend to agree and support the amendment, the concept of the International Monetary Fund and the Bretton Woods Agreements, with all the ramifications associated therewith. I think the minister does a disservice to this extent: he talks about "subscription" as though we are dealing with an ordinary bank where you make an investment and as time goes by your equity increases or you recover your investment. It would be more frank to point out that any money we put in under the Bretton Woods Agreements and into the IMF is a gift: we are never going to get it back. There is no way we can get it back with inflation going the way it is and the dire circumstances of the people who are doing most of the borrowing.
It is a gift. We'should not back off from saying that because we have a responsibility to do something to help other parts of the world. In the short run, I do not think Canada really needs to be associated with the Bretton Woods Agreements. It is of no benefit to us in the short run, because the world is not just short run. There is a much bigger picture than that. In the long run it is in Canada's interest to have a stable world economy and a stable world generally. To that extent, any of the international agreements we enter into are important and will serve us in the future.
When I say "in the short run", the one occasion I can recall on which we had to go and get assistance-I think it was during the 1962 campaign when another party formed the government-I could never understand why in the world we ever put ourselves into that kind of a position with the International Monetary Fund. To have to go on our knees, as we did at that time, to beg and plead for support, and then, as a humiliating condition of that support, to be locked into a fixed exchange rate, was the worst possible position for Canada to be placed in. Why we did not simply allow the dollar to depreciate and find its own level, without accepting that kind of external discipline, I do not know. It took us a number of years to break out of that fixed exchange rate position and finally get back to a floating exchange rate. I presume those events took place because the debate was in that third official language-"hustings"-and that people were just scared out of their wits at the idea the Canadian dollar would drop below par and slip from its high of $1.05 U.S. to around $0.92 U.S.

That was exactly the remedy which was required for the situation Canada found itself in at that particular time. So when we are talking about this "hustings" language, it is not just hon. members on my right who use that language. Hon. members opposite used it during that campaign and I think it was very unfortunate and unfair way which added nothing to the solution of Canada's problems.
It is true, as the hon. member for York-Simcoe said, that one of the effects of the amendment to the Bretton Woods Agreements will be to do away with the standard, with the discipline. But in my view it is time we did so. There is more than that involved, to this extent: what bothers me as much as anything about these international agreements is the weight we give to the form of an agreement. We think that because we have entered into an agreement of some sort, we have in fact solved a problem. That is just not true. No matter what kind of an agreement we make-and some agreement is better than no agreement-I support international agreements. But we have to be realistic. What serves the world is not agreements, but an understanding of economics and a willingness among countries to play their role in world economics.
I would just like to give one example. Probably the greatest outstanding success in terms of a country raising itself from nowhere and pulling itself up is China, which is not a signatory to any of these agreements. It does not benefit from the Bretton Woods Agreements; it does not benefit from the International Monetary Fund; it did not receive Marshall aid. No matter what you name, China did not benefit from any of it. The great success of the Chinese Republic is in its determination and its leadership which set out to do something.
What I am saying is that simply to set up these organizations and simply trying to be internationally good citizens- and I think we have to do that even at the risk of failing-does not solve anything. We should not really place too much reliance on that. What the world skirts by placing this emphasis on formal agreements is the kind of problem that the Chinese did not skirt. Just as in our own country we are not going to solve the problem of unemployment or the problem of inadequate purchasing power by passing legislation or setting up boards of one kind or another, we cannot do it internationally, either.
If we are to solve our problems here in Canada, the only way I can see at the moment of doing so is to ensure a substantial redistribution of income-and this is equally true internationally. No matter what few dollars we put in-I should not say "few dollars" because I do not want to be charged with saying $27 million or $28 million is a few dollars-but in relative terms, compared to the wealth of Canada, the amount of money we are to contribute to the IMF and to our responsibilities under Bretton Woods is not going to put a dent into the problems of the Third World or those countries which need our assistance. Unless there is redistribution of income between the rich of the world and the poor, there is no solution either in Bretton Woods Agreements or in the International Monetary Fund. However, it does give the
May 24, 1977

opportunity of freeing us from the restriction and discipline of gold.
I would like to deal with some of the ten points which the hon. member for York-Simcoe raised. In many ways I feel 1 should compliment him because, although I do not agree with him, as he would expect-he would be horrified if I did-I do want to compliment him on giving a lot of thought to explaining his position. I would also like to congratulate his ghost writer, who I am sure had a substantial role to play in preparing the extensive notes which the hon. member used in his speech. I do not say this to denigrate in any way the important and substantial contribution the hon. member has made. 1 recognize, however, that to dredge up all those Cassandra-like utterances requires more than the work of one man, no matter how energetic he may be.

One hon. member says that is not a bad idea. Let us just look at that. There is a tendency for all these monetarists to say that the problem of inflation is just a mechanical one-a too large money supply. How, then, does one explain what is happening in Canada at the moment, when the Bank of Canada, even severely restricting the money supply to the natural growth, cannot give the money away? It cannot even increase the money supply to the point to which it said it wished to increase the money supply.
The reason is that the economy is so flat that there is no reason to increase the money supply, because it has nowhere to go. If, indeed, it is the increase in the money supply which causes inflation, we should surely be down to zero inflation, because if we look at the money supply it is the lowest it has ever been with the kind of inflation to which we are subject at the moment. 1 am not discounting the fact that the money supply does play a role in this. Almost everything plays a role in inflation, but it is only those who really do not want to think about the economy but who live to latch on to some particular aspect who give the money supply situation such weight. I do not really want to be like Switzerland. The hon. member for York-Simcoe was holding Switzerland out as a model. As admirable a country as it might be, and as admirable a people as the Swiss may be, I really do not fancy Canada having the kind of laws and tax havens which tend to look the other way when it comes to money or when it comes to bank accounts and say, "It is not our business what happens to them." Money has certain connotations attached to it, connotations which cannot be disregarded.
Bretton Woods Agreements
I do not really see this as a model for us. I would like to deal with some of the ten points that the hon. member for York-Simcoe put forth today. I must say, in fairness, that I did not catch all of the ten points-two of them eluded me completely. Points 1 and 5 were, I found, merely repetition. But 10 is such a goodly number, and amongst my people we place a lot of importance on 10 of anything. I presume the hon. member for York-Simcoe was trying to emulate that in some fashion, although I must say he did not emulate one thing, because it would take an awfully big rock to carve all the words that he mouthed today, and I do not know that we have quite that much marble around or that much time to put all the engraving on it.
The great point that was being made by the hon. member for York-Simcoe was that the world should subject itself to discipline. This is an argument that I have heard and perhaps one of the arguments that induced me to become a socialist and certainly to take a part in politics, that is the idea of discipline. I think discipline is important, and certainly selfdiscipline and national discipline are important, but all too often it is a euphemism that is applied to the poor when one says, "If only you were disciplined, you would be all right".
I am tempted to say that we must have some discipline in some of these poor countries, but to say that they are poor because they do not have discipline is to ignore everything else such as history, gifts of nature, and all the other things that distinguish between the rich and the poor. That somebody is born rich, better off, or clever is no example of their own self-discipline, only of their good luck and fortune-and it is the other way round as well. Who are we going to discipline by staying with the gold standard and saying that gold shall be the basis on which you get credit or you do not get credit? You will not discipline the rich, because they have gold, but the poor who do not have gold.
What we are trying to do in a small way-and I entered my reservations about the Bretton Woods Agreements and the IMF-is to move away from mercantilism, the international mercantilism of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries where gold was thought to be the answer, where the accumulation of gold by a nation was supposed to be a measure of wealth. What Adam Smith said-and I am quoting a good conservative economist, yet one who seems to be terribly misunderstood-is that the wealth of nations does not consist of gold but of their ability to produce and to do the kinds of things that human beings are capable of doing.
Why, then, do we have to restrict the world to using gold as the criterion, to going back to a mercantilist world, a world in which the poor will never have a chance because they are not lucky enough to be born on a gold mine? We certainly do not want that. If risks attend this-and I pointed out that there are risks associated with what we are doing and that in fact we may not succeed in what we are doing, and if we do, we may not succeed in any great way-it is certainly worth trying. It is certainly better than sticking to a standard which the poor have no hope of even coming close to and which deprives them

May 24, 1977
Bretton Woods Agreements
of any hope at all. At least this way there is some kind of chance.
We should have an independent mind in this country. What is an independent mind? Is it that charity begins at home, to heck with what happens in the rest of the world, let us look after ourselves first, let us solve our own problems before we deal with somebody else's problems? Are we ever going to solve our own problems? Are we ever going to have enough for ourselves? I think the answer must be "no". We are better off now than most countries of the world, yet many of us say, "Oh, well, we are still not well off enough and we cannot help anyone else until we are better off than we are now".
We will never get to a point in human history where society has every single thing it wants. At some point, regardless of the problems that are facing society, you have to be prepared to help other people as well. In the long run-and I think history will bear this out-the poor and the rich cannot live side by side: sooner or later the pressure of the poor on the rich will destroy the rich, and the only way of averting that is to ensure that the world is not divided into those two camps and at least an attempt is made to move one closer to the other.
I do not know whether the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Roche) attends the same caucus meetings as the hon. member for York-Simcoe, whether they talk to each other, whether they have the same leader, whether they are in the same political party. He can put together all kinds of figures which have no meaning whatsoever, so he is highly qualified to be a minister of finance. I am sure he can wear a pair of new shoes as beautifully as our present Minister of Finance, or as the former minister of finance who graced that office and who is honouring the House today with his presence. If the hon. member for York-Simcoe were minister of finance, and if he were to see the provinces and their agencies going to the American market for borrowings, would he institute capital controls? Would he tell the provinces, "No, you cannot go"? Would he say to Hydro Quebec that it could not go to the American market? Would he say to the Manitoba government that it could not borrow for its projects? Would he say to the government of Ontario-and he might be listened to in this case-that Ontario could not borrow for hydro purposes in the American market?
Would the hon. member for York-Simcoe say to Arctic Gas Pipe Line Company that it could not borrow money in the United States to build any more pipelines in Canada? Or would he go further than that and say that no more pipelines could be built in Canada because there are not enough domestic savings? Even if we were to give everything the hon. member has suggested to the business community, we still would not have enough money to build pipelines, and we would have to import that capital.
On the other hand, does the hon. member not see that much of the foreign capital which is brought into this country is brought in because of the high value of the Canadian dollar and high interest rates? One does not offset the other. I think that because money is brought into this country our dollar tends to stay up. If the hon. member were minister of finance, would he set up a foreign exchange board, and would he say that from now on a province or provincial agency cannot borrow more than $50,000 outside the country without his approval or without the approval of a board which he would reluctantly set up because he does not like boards? Would the hon. member do that? Unless he is prepared to do so, while there may be some valid criticism directed toward the federal government, that is not the total picture of what is wrong with the economy. I do not think the hon. member's argument really adds in any substantial way, beyond its political connotations, to solving the problems of this country.
My time is drawing to a close: I have a few more minutes left and I want to deal with another question which always arises in these debates. There is no doubt that the present government has been inept. There is no doubt that this government has made all kinds of mistakes and is still making them. This government has its priorities all wrong and its social values all screwed up. But something else should be added to this debate, and that is that when something goes wrong in the country, it is not the fault of just the government. In fact, we have to look at the people who took the advice of the government and elected it, because the government certainly did not steal its way to power. It was voted in and it continues to maintain a fair amount of support. Part of the responsibility rests with the ordinary people of Canada. Problems are not created just by governments, whether they be provincial or
Adjournment Motion
federal. Problems are not created just by political parties, whether it be my party, my hon. friend's party or the government party. As a nation we are not doing well. Part of the reason is that we are badly governed, but another part of the reason is that people are not responding to the call to harder work.
We have had it pretty soft in this country, and we have been far too prone to keep blaming the other guy instead of looking at ourselves and admitting that part of the responsibility is our own. Perhaps what ultimately must be said is that this kind of malaise should never be ascribed to the people but, rather, to political parties. The government has the chief responsibility because it is the governing party and it is supposed to assume leadership. It has a responsibility to speak out and to call upon people to do the kinds of things necessary to get this country running again. The official opposition also has a responsibility to speak. It should not merely attack the government on this issue or that, or use selected facts to make it look as though nobody else is involved. I touched on that when I referred to the provinces.
My party has a responsibility which I think it is trying to live up to. That responsibility is to try to put the whole thing into some kind of perspective and to argue the morality of the situation, especially when it comes to something like the Bretton Woods Agreements, which is more than just a technical agreement or a technical document. We need to have a moral look at the world in order to understand the significance of the agreement and to argue the points involved.
