speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO EXEMPT INTEREST ON MUNICIPAL BONDS
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of amending the Income Tax Act to exempt the interest of municipal bonds from income tax.
He said: Mr. Speaker, first I wish to thank hon. colleagues on all sides of the House for unanimously agreeing to make the change which was made this afternoon and to allow me to present a motion standing in my name rather than the bill which has been standing in my name for some time. In fairness, I must say that I intend to leave the bill to die on the order paper since the government has undertaken, through legislation brought into this House, to cover the majority of the points I had requested. It would seem to me, therefore, that there would be no purpose in leaving it on the order paper.
[DOT] (UOO)
The motion that I propose this afternoon has just been read, but I am going to read it again. It is very brief and I think it carries a lot of weight. It reads as follows:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of amending the Income Tax Act to exempt the interest of municipal bonds from income tax.
I want to begin by quoting from remarks made by the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) in a speech to the Canadian Federation of Municipalities in Toronto on May 18. I am, of course, quoting out of context but I am sure the excerpts are capable of standing alone. He said:
I am deeply concerned about the high level of taxes-of all kinds-that the individual Canadian pays to school boards, municipal, provincial and federal governments. To this end, I stand prepared to press for meaningful reform of the municipal finance situation.
Later in the same speech he said:
As an immediate action, it is my intention to ensure that federal programs will be better able to respond to the needs and concerns of Canadians living in all types of municipalities, large and small, rural and urban, and that federal programs will be more flexible in taking account of the fiscal circumstances of municipalities.
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Turner).]
Also, given the way I perceive the problem, I am prepared to consider any reasonable suggestion to bring forward a reform of the municipal Finance situation.
In a very interesting speech to an important group of municipal representatives the minister said he was "prepared to press for" in one case, and in the second case, "to bring forward a reform of the municipal finance situation." That is what my motion is about, Mr. Speaker. I suggest that taking away the federal tax on the interest on municipal bonds will make a major change in the municipal finance situation.
I have to be slightly critical of a couple of the minister's comments, however. He referred to a statement he had made in Alberta in February of this year where he raised three possible avenues of assistance to cities in order to keep pace with providing adequate municipal services. He listed these as follows:
(1)	increasing federal assistance programs for such projects as home rehabilitation, neighbourhood improvement and sewage treatment;
(2)	transferring funds to the provinces under the condition that the money be passed along to municipalities; and
(3)	establishing a direct tax rebate system to reimburse Canadians for some of the heavy tax load they now bear.
The problem is that in the first of these items the federal government would envisage taking funds they have already taken from the taxpayers and turning them back to taxpayers. Everyone is aware that the federal government takes something like 40 per cent along the way in overhead. I suggest that leaving the tax money where it is would make more sense than taking it with one hand and giving it back with the other.
The second proposition of transferring funds to the provinces with a condition that they be passed along to municipalities is very similar to a grant that municipalities used to receive from the provinces with strings attached-providing the municipalities did certain things. The government of Ontario did away with that kind of grant many years ago simply because grants with strings attached have never been very successful.
This motion is a major change and a major improvement. It is not entirely radical; the United States has been doing it for years. It is forward thinking, however, and in my opinion would be supported by all municipalities in Canada. Let me outline what I think the five aims of my motion are. First, it would reduce municipal costs; second, reduce municipal taxes; third, reduce the Canadian balance of payments; fourth, provide excellent investment for Canadians in all walks of life and, finally, increase federal taxes. I will deal with these one at a time.
The first is in regard to reducing municipal taxes. In his speech the minister referred to the debt costs of municipalities ranging from 10 to 20 per cent of their total budget. If we could cut back by removing the taxes on interest, of course, the interest would be much lower, probably ranging between 5 and 7 per cent instead of the 10 or 11 Vi per cent it has been running at. The savings compounded as the interest is compounded now would amount of half the debt service charges in time.
May 24, 1977

The second thing is the reduction of municipal taxes. Many members of this House have been involved with municipal councils over the years. I have spent more time on municipal councils than in this House. Members know that municipal taxes are only raised to meet costs; the municipal field does not have the ability to raise taxes for such extravagant programs as Canada Works, Local Initiative Programs and such things as that. Municipalities can only raise taxes to meet their obligations and do those things which are absolutely necessary. If the cost to municipalities by way of interest on their debentures could be reduced, they would turn that money back to the taxpayers either in reduced taxes or extended services. Just recently the city of Belleville passed its annual budget, and after much discussion added an extra quarter million dollars for repair to roads because it was found they were much below the standard for the province. That quarter million dollars could be doubled or tripled if their debt service charge were cut back.
What I have said so far is primarily the concern of municipalities. I hope my motion will be considered by the federal government, and therefore I must show there is some merit in it. One of the things that I think is most important is the reduction of our balance of payments. In discussion of Bill C-18, my colleague the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) expressed serious concern about the balance of payments. I would like to repeat many of the things he said, but I do not have the time. He made the point that countries with a high inflation rate, such as Canada, face high interest rates. That has been the case with municipalities, in their recent issues of debentures.
I have found from my research that municipalities, because they face large capital requirements and high domestic interest rates, have relied increasingly on foreign capital markets to meet their financing requirements. I have also found that a substantial proportion of net new issues are met with United States dollars. At the risk of boring the House I shall mention some statistics. Their source is the Bank of Canada Review, February, 1977, table 32, page S.71. I shall begin with 1973 figures, then quote figures pertaining to the last four years.
In 1973, the total gross issue of debentures amounted to $738 million, of which only 15 per cent was to be retired in other currencies. The figure in 1974 increased to $870 million, of which 27 per cent was to be retired in a foreign currency. The figure in 1975 increased to $1,417 million, of which 38 per cent was to be retired in a foreign currency. In 1976 the figure increased to $1,568 million, of which 52.5 per cent was to be retired in a foreign currency.
If one examines the foreign currency figures, one finds that in 1973 only 7 per cent of such obligations were to be retired in the currency of the United States. The figure jumped dramatically in 1974 to 29 per cent. In 1975 it reached 43 per cent, and in 1976 it reached 59 per cent. Clearly, the interest which flows to the United States returns not one cent in taxes to the Canadian federal government. Therefore, the Canadian feder-
Income Tax Act
al government would lose nothing if it did not collect taxes on the interest paid by municipalities.
I was speaking of gross issues just now. My figures show that in 1976, 67 per cent of all new issues, almost $478 million worth, were in United States dollars. Let me make a point to my colleagues from Quebec. Naturally I, being from Ontario and having been involved for many years in the Ontario municipal system, am familiar with that system. I point out to my colleagues from Quebec that the situation in Quebec is even worse than it is in Ontario. I refer to the table "Net new issues of municipalities by provinces" compiled from the banking and analysis section of the Bank of Canada. In 1973, of the total $398 million-odd in net new issues, only 27 per cent was for Ontario, whereas 59 per cent was for Quebec. Of that, 20 per cent was a foreign issue.
Although I do not have all the latest figures before me, I point out that this figure has increased dramatically. Quebec's share of total Canadian new issues in 1974 increased to 63 per cent, of which 45 per cent was in U.S. dollars. That proportion in 1975 increased to 67 per cent, of which 44 per cent was payable in U.S. dollars. Although the figure dropped somewhat in 1976, I point out that 34 per cent of the Quebec issue was in foreign issue. From Quebec, $195 million went to foreign sources in 1976 to cover Quebec municipal financing. The federal government received absolutely no return as tax from that distribution of funds.
I return to my five points. Many Canadians are looking for safe ways to invest their money. We talk of "Mother Bell" as issuing safe, blue chip stocks. I suggest that the municipalities of Canada are equally safe investments. If one could buy their bonds without having to pay tax on the interest one receives such investments would be most attractive to all types of people.
This brings me to my last point, that such a tax exemption would actually increase federal taxes. When the former minister of finance heard of this idea, he turned it down flat on the ground that the benefit would accrue only to the wealthy in Canada. I refute that contention. Handled properly, this kind of investment would be available to unions, retirement funds, insurance companies and private individuals, rich or poor-in other words, to a cross-section of Canadian life. Further, the money paid in interest would stay in Canada and not go to some foreign country. While no tax would be levied directly on the interest paid, the money spent in this country would indirectly generate taxes. The people who are paid interest by the municipalities would spend the money on goods and services. The federal government could levy a tax on these goods and services. If a municipal government decides to provide more services with the money it saves, it is clear that the money will be spent on labour, with respect to which the government would levy income tax and on goods and services on which the government levies a sales tax of approximately 12 per cent.
If hon. members are not yet convinced that the federal government would actually receive more money if it decided not to tax the interest on municipal bonds, I could reinforce

May 24, 1977
Income Tax Act
my argument with many more details and figures. Unfortunately, I do not have much time remaining. In the few minutes remaining I wish to quote a passage from Douglas Fullerton's book, "Provincial and Municipal Financing". On page 293, Mr. Fullerton quotes a Mr. Calvert who, speaking of the United States, wrote:
The tax exemption for interest on municipal bonds is essential to state and local government, not only to obtain a much lower rate of interest on these bonds than would be obtained without such tax exemption, but more basically to protect their independent sovereignty under our dual state-federal system of government.
That point must be borne in mind. I also quote the words of Mr. Patrick Mahoney who, writing on the role of the Canadian government in municipal finance, said in part:
There is no easy way that the federal government can intervene directly to improve sources of municipal finance. The British North America Act gives the federal government authority to raise taxes by any means whatever. Provincial governments can levy direct taxes only and can, of course, delegate to municipal governments all or part of that right. The federal government can delegate nothing directly to municipalities.
My motion suggests a legal and attractive way for the federal government to give the municipalities a piece of the federal action. Our municipalities desperately need such relief, which would be of benefit to overburdened municipal taxpayers who pay, with residential taxes, about 45 per cent of all municipal taxes. Our municipalities desperately need the relief which the federal government could provide without interfering with the rights of the provinces. They merely have to back off of one form of interest. I suggest it would do all of those many things that I have outlined.
I want to close with a very brief comment to my colleagues on the other side. Over this past year it has been my privilege and my willingness to allow a number of private members' bills and motions to pass through this House. I have personally made sure that consent was given. I have not lobbied on this matter one bit. 1 have not asked anyone that it be given consent. However, I suggest through you, Mr. Speaker, to those who are responsible that this is the way in which the federal government can make an excellent contribution to municipalities in all of Canada. I suggest to them that they might reciprocate.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO EXEMPT INTEREST ON MUNICIPAL BONDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I congratulate the hon. member for Hastings (Mr. Ellis) for raising this most important matter. If the hon. member's bill were worded in a way that asked that this matter go to committee to investigate various ways and means of assisting the municipalities, I would be very much in support of it. However, since the bill restricts itself to only one rather unhappy method, I am not in the position to support the bill, as admirable as the intention of the hon. member for Hastings may be. I will give my reasons for that.
I have been a municipal councillor. I realize that some of the things the hon. member brings to the attention of this House are so. However, as a municipal councillor it has been my experience that the greatest benefit that people receive from
[Mr. Ellis.)
their taxes is at the municipal level. I cannot think of any kind of tax that people pay for which they receive more services. I realize that taxes are quite high. However, we must realize what we get for them: education, police protection, fire protection, sanitary services, roads, welfare and social services, recreational services and housing services. I could go on. I do not know of any area of government in which the benefits are greater for the taxes paid.
There is one essential problem with municipal taxation. Of all taxes, including sales tax-because there are exemptions in sales tax-the most regressive are at the municipal level. If this measure were put into effect, would it reduce the regressiveness of the municipal taxes? It would not. It would lower the whole level of municipal taxes but the essential regressiveness would still remain. We would increase the total regressiveness of the system if taxes were not collected on municipal bonds. I will come to this matter of who collects it and the kind of revenues they get from it. I argue, in fact, that it would be transferred to the income tax. What we would be doing is taking this tax and making it a larger burden on someone else. I do not think it would be done, because the income tax is not as progressive as it should be.
The other point I would like to make is that the small bond buyer is already allowed a deduction of $1,000 a year. I do not know of very many people in the lower and middle income levels who collect more than the $1,000 in interest to which they are already exempt. The chief beneficiaries would be the very wealthy.
I am not suggesting that the hon. member for Hastings is doing it for that reason. I know him well enough to suggest that he is not. I know that his genuine concern is to find some way of helping the municipalities. However, I suggest this is the wrong and most costly way of doing it. This would help the very rich. In the United States, municipal bonds are a favourite tax haven of the rich. The suggestion made by every tax lawyer and tax accountant-

speechtext: And the big international unions.

speechtext:
It may to the extent that they are rich, too. I will not quarrel with that. I merely say "the rich", without singling out whether they are an organization, individual or whatever. Nevertheless, the point is the same. It is regressive.
If we are going to help the municipalities, surely we can find a better way than bringing in a regressive measure. There are ways of helping the people in municipalities. We are not talking about some coat of arms, as lovely as that may be: we are talking about the people who live in a city. The greatest help we ever provide to people in the cities is when we encourage senior citizens's housing and public housing. You can be selective in the sense of who you want to help. Not everyone in the city finds the taxes onerous. Wealthy people in the city are quite well off compared to poor people in the city. If we are to provide assistance, we should be more selective.
In view of the arguments the hon. member's party have made over the year about selectivity and helping, I thought he would have stayed away from these broad-axe approaches.
May 24, 1977

While they would be of some benefit to people in middle income groups, they would have a tendency to transfer their liabilities. Instead of the municipality having the tax to pay, the individual would have to pay it in some other way, probably in a more heavy way.
I want to deal with the central point of the hon. member's intervention. He stated we would not deprive the federal government of any revenue because, as I understood him, the money is raised externally. That would be true if the investment supply were totally elastic; in other words, if you had an investment supply that did not have any limits. We know that the investment pool is roughly of so many dollars. To the extent that you invest here, you do not invest somewhere else; you do not increase the pool of investment funds by providing additional investment opportunities. To the extent that you encourage one kind of investment by granting tax advantages, you simply shift from other sources.
At the moment, municipalities find it more advantageous to go to the American market in order to float their bonds. If it were more advantageous for the Canadian taxpayer to buy the municipal bonds, what would they do? They would buy them. There is no doubt that if you offered this kind of an advantage, there would be a flood into municipal bonds. Where would they get the money? They would take it out of other investments, investments in industry. The money is invested, no matter where it is. Even if it goes to a bank, the bank invests it. There is really no such thing as putting money in a mattress. There is really no money there. Most money is employed in one way or another.
To the extent that you provide an attraction for one kind of investment, you take it from another investment. Does the hon. member want to take investment out of industry, and thereby have all of our industry go to the United States, giving up ownership of our industry as well? If we have to go to the United States to borrow funds, the best thing to do is borrow in debt rather than sell out our industry as equity. That would be the consequence.
The argument that the federal government would not be disadvantaged from the tax point of view is only true if there is an unlimited supply of investment funds. However, there is not an unlimited supply of investment funds. What you get is a transfer of funds from one type of investment to another, depending on where the tax benefit is the greatest.
There is something else I want to argue against. We went through, and are still in it to some extent, this business of distortions in the tax systems. There are so many distortions and loopholes which encourage the government to move from one kind of investment to another.
What the Carter commission reported essentially was that a buck is a buck; that all income should be treated the same for taxation purposes. One important argument which they used, aside from the equity argument-which is a fair argument because from the equity point of view the people who benefit are the rich, not the poor-was that economically you set up
Income Tax Act
distortion in capital markets. We have this distortion now. Some of it is deliberate. For instance, the government creates distortion through the tax credit system to encourage Canadians to invest in Canadian equities. There is distortion in the sense that some companies are encouraged to invest in mining, such investment being written off as a result of the last budget. Our whole tax system is riddled with this kind of distortion, and all of it is bad.
This kind of distortion over the long term is bad because when you channel money into one area you tend to say, "Instead of removing this distortion we must give higher bonuses in some other area to attract more money". Who suffers as a result? The federal government is the main sufferer, but provincial income tax also suffers. To the extent this revenue is diminished we have to take one of two courses; either we increase taxes or we reduce services.
It has been argued that many services can be done away with, and usually the example of Information Canada is given. Now we have got rid of Information Canada we do not hear very much about what kind of government services we are going to eliminate. In truth the really costly government services are in the form of transfer payments to individuals, rather than bodies like Information Canada. 1 do not think any political party, regardless of what is said on the hustings, would be prepared to dismantle the social welfare system in Canada today, with our old age security, family allowances and all the rest.
Therefore it seems to me that while the intent of the bill is admirable, and I welcome it because it would instruct the committee to look at ways and means whereby municipalities could be assisted by this form of tax exemption, I think the hon. member for Hastings would create, were the bill to receive approval of the House, very serious distortions in investment patterns, great inequity in terms of who gets the benefit, and ultimately the bill would be of no help to people in municipalities in that the money saved would go to the wrong people.

The exemption of interest on municipal bonds from income tax would convey benefits which would vary greatly among provinces. response to any financing problems which municipalities may have.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to add my words to the debate on the motion of the hon. member for Hastings. It is a very worth-while motion, but one that must not be dealt with in isolation. In this sense I follow the prescription as outlined by the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge (Mr. Saltsman).
I will be brief because I know there is not much time left, and the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Kaplan) is most interested in this subject and would like to make a comment on it. Looking at the motion in the context of federal-provincial fiscal arrangements, it is implicit in the speech of the hon. member for Hastings that since the war provincial and municipal governments have been asked to take on an ever-increasing load of responsibility. I am referring to social responsibilities, and they need the financing to discharge their responsibilities.
In the 1960's there was a movement afoot, prompted by the social revolution in Quebec, toward more decentralization of federal taxation power to the provinces. Mr. Pearson, the prime minister at the time, acquiesced in the face of very strong demands, not only from Quebec but from Ontario and other provinces, and allowed more taxation revenues to go to the provinces to pay for increased social commitments. Ten years later, in 1977, we see across this country a popular movement, which is not a movement on behalf of the general public, but one stemming from provincial politicians and provincial public servants who say, "Look, the only way to keep this country together is for us to decentralize more, for the provinces to have more taxation revenues and more powers".
Income Tax Act
As far as I am concerned, this kind of approach and direction toward Canada's future is fraught with danger.
The hon. member for Hastings talked about municipalities having to go to New York and overseas for finances. In Ontario, his colleague, who is seeking re-election, Mr. Davis, has been to Germany and Italy to get money for the province. We have seen a trend where municipal and provincial governments have borrowed money outside of the country. I agree it is a harmful thing for the Canadian economy.
Coming back to my theme in terms of federal-provincial relations, before we agree to a motion of this kind, the federal government and the provinces have to sit down to determine if borrowing by municipal and provincial governments abroad is in the best interests of Canada, before we talk about the general expenditures themselves. In the last couple of years Canada has become the most indebted nation in the world in terms of foreign borrowing. Implicit in the motion of the hon. member for Hastings is the fact that he wants us to continue in this vein. I am saying no. Before we take a piecemeal approach, as he is indicating, we should sit down at a constitutional conference to tidy up our Constitution and to eliminate the overlapping where the federal government intrudes on provincial jurisdiction. We should cut the costs and the waste there. We should not look only at transferring money to the municipalities, but we should say to the provinces and the municipalities, "Don't you think there are some fields of social policy and governmental policy where it would be better to divest authority in the federal government?"
I would like to refer to the example of education. It is unrealistic, at this moment, to think the federal government, by agreement with the provinces, could gain a greater role in education. I am not talking about post-secondary education; I am talking about lower education. This is relative to the motion, because in the province of Ontario and throughout Canada education costs are borne by the municipal taxpayers. I suppose we should go back to 1867 and the Fathers of Confederation. They gave jurisdiction over education to the provinces. In retrospect, some of the problems in this country with respect to national unity, the lack of understanding, the continuation of the so-called two solitudes, may have arisen from that decision. Before we take a narrow view as taken by the hon. member for Hastings we should look at areas in which the federal government can assume powers, presently given to the provinces, in the national interest. Obviously, I do not want the federal government to run the education system of the country. But we must adopt a system similar to that which we developed in medicare in which the federal government sets national standards.
There is a degree of portability attached to medicare plans and we should make similar provisions in the field of education. At the present time, if parents must travel from one part of the country to another their children suffer serious dislocation because of changes in the education system from province to province. A federal presence in education would alleviate

May 24, 1977
Income Tax Act
the extent of this dislocation. It would also help the cause of national unity.
I am afraid my remarks have been somewhat disjointed. I thank you, Mr. Speaker, for allowing me to inject some of my concern about constitutional matters in the debate on the motion put forward by the hon. member for Hastings. But I believe a case can be made out for saying that motions of this kind ought not to be discussed in isolation but in the context of federal and provincial fiscal arrangements. Notwithstanding the hon. member's intentions, and I am sure they are sincere, I believe that sending this motion to a committee or acting upon it at this time would be premature.

speakeroldname: Mr. Bob Kaplan (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO EXEMPT INTEREST ON MUNICIPAL BONDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is not much time left to me but I am glad to have an opportunity to contribute to this discussion because I wish to put some figures before the House, but before I do so I should like to extend congratulations, as others have done, to the mover of this motion. It is obviously an important subject. Many members on our side wanted to speak, and there has been participation from all parties.
The question of municipal financing is an extremely difficult one. Although we have been elected to a level of government which does not have direct control over this area, we nevertheless represent people and we come from cities, towns and municipalities: we cannot help trying to use the authority of this level of government to lessen the burden borne by the municipalities in one way or another.
The hon. member for Hastings (Mr. Ellis) referred to a speech by the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Ouellet). I read that speech with interest and I noted that three or four suggestions were made regarding ways in which the federal fiscal power might be used to alleviate the burden on the municipalities. I must say, with respect to the minister, that I disagree with his approach. I do not think the federal government ought to alter its fiscal policies so as to support municipalities. I say this with a great deal of regret.
For the federal treasury the cities and municipalities of Canada are a great source of revenue. I have not looked at the figures but it would not surprise me to find that the bulk of the revenues of the federal government come from taxpayers, corporations and individuals, within the larger municipalities. Why is it that the federal government is able to find these corporations and individuals such a rich source of revenue while the municipalities cannot? What is it that the municipalities lack which prevents them having the same access as the federal government to the incomes and fortunes of Canadians? To ask that question is to answer it. They do not have the power to tax in the way the federal government does. Who can give them this power? Is it this parliament? It is not. It is the legislatures of the provinces which possess the authority necessary to give the municipalities the jurisdiction which would provide them with a proper tax base. But for one reason or another they have not done so. They have left their creatures, the municipalities, starved for funds.

Hon. members may ask themselves what is the reason for this inaction. I think it is because the provinces are afraid to see the municipalities possessed of an adequate tax base. That is why we in Ottawa are under such pressure to help them out. But we are in a level of government which cannot do it in any effective way. It is the provinces which can do it.
It we do allow exemptions from income tax on municipal bonds to individuals and various enterprises we shall only produce the kind of situation which has existed for many years in the United States. It certainly results in a lower interest cost to the municipalities. But what is the over-all effect? A number of hon. members have called attention to some of the results-the regional inequities inherent in such an approach, the bias in favour of individuals with high incomes, and so on.
