subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE SUBSCRIPTION TO INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND AND INTERNATIONAL BANK FOR CONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I now refer to the 1966 debate when we considered some major amendments to the Bretton Woods Agreements Act. I have here this evening the official report of the debates. Second reading was pro forma. The main debate on the resolution was held in April 1966. At that time, for any legislation entailing
May 24, 1977

some expenditure by the Canadian government there was a resolution, first reading, second reading, then consideration of the bill in committee and finally third reading.

Well, Mr. Speaker, it is very interesting to see why, going back to the debate of 1966 in which I participated on second reading. That debate was very short. A good deal more was said at the resolution stage. I would like to go back to that particular era in talking about this bill because I think that, notwithstanding that there have been changes in times, certainly there have been changes in the world situation.
I know there are some who believe that the Bretton Woods Agreement was written or inspired by the devil. To me that is totally false. Those of us who had the experience of pre-World War II monetary exchanges recall the absolute chaos, the dog-eat-dog atmosphere. As a matter of fact it was symptomatic of what was to come in 1939. It was just one of the symbols of one nation doing it to another as part of the so-called economic nationalism that came out of the economic depression of the 1930's. The world suffered as a result of World War II, there is no doubt about it, but then I would say that over the years 1933 to 1938 or 1939 as much human misery was inflicted on the world populace as a result of this international monetary warfare as was inflicted by the horrible ravages of war from 1939 to 1945. That latter part was measurable. At least one could put a finger upon it and seem to identify. At least there was a scapegoat for the suffering.
In 1937 I was a high school student travelling in Europe, and it was almost a daily joke to determine the value of the franc, the mark, the pound or the dollar as each tried to out-manoeuver the other. One of the hopeful lights of 1944 was the determination of men the world over, as they established the United Nations Charter and as everybody got hold of his good resolutions and put them back on the table, to start out with the Bretton Woods Agreement. Its original concept was modest, and I do not suppose under the circumstances-it being 30 years old-that one can quarrel with the decision that the United States dollar would be the primary reserve currency and that the pound sterling would be the second reserve or joint reserve currency. It worked for some considerable time. Oh, Canadians did not like it too much because our dollar was at a considerable discount to the United States dollar for a period. Then there were subtle changes. Of course they would be subtle changes; there is no such thing as a static situation in world international trade and commodity relations. Even the monetary market experience had some influences which, I think, by and large in the whole picture were wholesome effects of the checks and counter-checks to the excesses of a too rigid system dictated by men whose motives were not altogether altruistic.
We saw some changes in the 1950's. I remember in 1958 and 1959 being a member on the government side when there were minor changes in the levels of the membership subscriptions for Canada, and then in 1966 there was a wholesale
Bretton Woods Agreements
change. Circumstances had changed considerably. By then we had seen the emergence on an independent basis of many of what we call today the developing nations. The colonial system had started to come apart, I suppose through the impetus of the United Nations, and then because of any number of reasons. It may have been a calculated move on the part of the Soviet Union and the United States in their already apparent conflict over domination. Even today the United States attempts to impose North American style democracy on people who are not suited to it. If only they could make up their minds that what is good for Washington, Los Angeles, Chicago and New York is not necessarily good the world over!
Over the years there has been a great deal of strife. Western Europeans and North Americans have been trying to impose their brands of democracy on all the peoples of the world. Let them be a little bit humble. Let them realize that people will achieve their potential, possibly under a modified system of their own choice, but let us not have North American leaders trumpeting about the world saying that all countries must assume a North American brand of democracy, because that will only fail.
On the other side, the Soviet Union has been very eager to obtain recruits for its views in the United Nations. So therefore we had a great rush in the 1960's and early 1970's to foment independence in many countries which were not ready for independence. Their economies and the development of their peoples have actually retrogressed as a result of this too hasty run into the so-called world economic race.
I remember the Commonwealth Parliamentary Association Confederation in Wellington, New Zealand, in 1965, and subsequent conferences, and I particularly remember when the Bretton Woods Agreement was amended formally to establish special drawing rights. Special drawing rights were on the International Monetary Fund side, but the mechanism for loans at low rates of interest to developing countries-in other words, that effort by developed countries to assist those who, in many instances, were pitchforked into the post-mid-twentieth century-was the World Bank.
However, immediately many of these countries looked upon special drawing rights as the teats on a prolific sow, another source from which to draw. Never mind that this in itself was doing damage to some of the countries concerned and that the funds that they might thereby draw would not be destined for the general improvement of their people, the Bretton Woods Agreement established one base reserve currency. Incidentally, there is not one comma, not one dot on an i nor one bar on a t which this parliament can change with respect to that agreement as presented in this bill. There are changes to the limits of Canada's qualifications, and this time there is formal inclusion in a bill rather than using a one dollar item as was done in 1970, and again in 1972, with regard to special drawing rights. There is an increase or change in the level of Canada's subscription, and also the determination of the value of the U. S. dollar as of July 1, 1944. These things are all now being crystalized and formalized in this particular bill.

May 24, 1977
Bretton Woods Agreements
We see the extent of Canada's commitment in the amendments to proposed new section 5 of the act. In proposed new section 6 there is a method whereby at a particular date Canada's commitment to the International Monetary Fund, its subscription, the value of its special drawing rights and any other commitments it may have-I can spell them out, for instance from the specification to the $1 item in the Appropriation Act No. 1, 1970, Vote L37b. This item reads as follows:
To authorize the Minister of Finance to provide for payment out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund to the International Monetary Fund in the current and subsequent Fiscal years, in addition to the amounts authorized by the Bretton Woods Agreements Act, a sum of money equivalent to the increase in Canada's quota of $360,000,000 (U.S.) of which $90,000,000 (U.S.) shall be in gold, $3,600,000 (U.S.) in Canadian currency and $266,400,000 (U.S.) in non-interest bearing non-negotiable demand notes in Canadian currency, in such form as may be determined by the Minister of Finance, and to authorize the Minister of Finance to provide for payment out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund in the current and subsequent fiscal years, in addition to the amounts authorized by the Bretton Woods Agreements Act, a sum of money equivalent to $149,800,000 (U.S.) for the purchase of 1,498 shares of stock of the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development, being in addition to Canada's subscription as a member thereof, of which a portion may be paid in cash, a portion in gold, and, pending cash requirements by the Bank, a portion in non-interest bearing non-negotiable demand notes, in such form as may be determined by the Minister of Finance.
Incidentally, Mr. Speaker, the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development referred to was the precursor of the World Bank.
That excerpt refers in part to what we are ratifying tonight.
The minister indicated in his remarks this afternoon that more and more there is a non-reliance on gold. Since 1966 when I participated in the committee hearings and in the debates at all stages of Bill C-144, which Bill C-18 purports to amend, there have been some changes. First of all, 1 think there was a fudamental change in the Bretton Woods Agreement in the effectiveness of the U.S. dollar as the base currency reserve because of the problems of 1970-71 in the United States. At that time the United States government was faced with the dilemma of unemployment and a run on its dollar. In order to stimulate its dollar the United States economy would have had to lower the interest rates. There were hundreds of millions, if not billions, of Euro-dollars chasing around Europe and elsewhere, arising out of Marshall aid and the continuation of the United States generosity in the rebuilding of Europe and Japan. This money, which had been invested in the United States at the then higher interest rates, of course took flight when interest rates were lowered to stimulate the domestic economy and was chasing higher interest in other parts of the world.
The picture repeats itself here in Canada. It repeated itself in Australia. It is such a familiar picture to those who understand a little bit about international monetary relations that it has become somewhat dreary-not only dreary but distressing to see the same mistakes repeated time and time again.
We saw the United States abandon the fixed price of $35 per ounce for gold. As a result of certain pressures from South Africa, the Soviet Union, France and others, the price of gold

went crazy. It went to $170 per ounce and possibly higher. Some people paid $200 per ounce. That bubble burst, although the price is still well in excess of $35 per ounce, but then so it should be considering all the factors. It is much closer to reality than it was two years ago, however.
We have the unsolved problem of Euro-dollars chasing Euro-dollars and ending up in the pockets of a number of OPEC countries.
This whole situation has been turned around. The agreement to which reference is made in Bill C-18 does not in any way represent the situation today. The agreement was arrived at after a great deal of patient work and concessions. It had to apply all over the world and some people had to have their arms twisted behind their backs-there is no doubt about it. Cognizance had to be taken of countries, like Canada, which wanted to belong to the club, signed the request for membership, and then stepped outside. Since 1970, instead of being a regulated current account, we have applied ourselves to maintaining a fixed relationship with a base currency. For the second time Canada has said, "This does not apply to us. We belong to the IMF, but do not think we are going to be caught as we were in 1962, trying to maintain a fixed relationship."
Of course we have gone through crises. In 1962 there was a crisis. The Canadian dollar had been away over-priced and the world suddenly came up with the definitive answer, abetted by the then Minister of Finance who knew that our trade could only recover if our dollar came down. Certain aspects of that, I found, related to the economic nationalism of 1935 and the years before that.
In 1968 we had an even worse crisis, if the truth be known. It is only apologists for the then Liberal administration in the media who have failed to tell the people of Canada this true state of affairs with regard to that financial crisis of 1968. There was a deliberate suppression of information. It was available to the then Leader of the Opposition who, like the statesman he was, refused to engage in certain tactics which, while they might have been of some advantage politically to him and those of us who were his supporters, would have meant but a pyrrhic victory in so far as the Canadian economic system was concerned. It would have gone flat broke.
During the last year we saw a drive against the Canadian dollar, undertaken for certain reasons. Incidentally, I am not a great lover, a great admirer, of the Bretton Woods Agreements. I think it is too rigid. I think a creeping average was called for, an average outside the limits where it would have been possible to make money from arbitrage. At present such fixed limits for people involved in arbitrage are merely a licence to print money. We are on a so-called float right now, but few people in the world can afford to go back to the jungle of the 1930's.
Flow many people can adjust to measures for preserving order? When you introduce such measures some immediately say, "We are not going to abide by the rules." We have seen some highly questionable devaluations motivated purely by
May 24, 1977

economic advantage and the thought of doing your neighbour "in the eye." To me that is distressing, far more distressing than some of the regulations it has been necessary to impose on some developing countries which think capital and revenue are merged in one and can be eaten at the same meal.
When this bill is before the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs I hope we shall be able to have the kind of discussion we had in March and April, 1966, with Department of Finance specialists in international relations. Let them explain to us the exact meaning of some of the terms we are discussing, because I do not think any member of this House is expert enough to say exactly what is meant by the term "International Monetary Fund," or by "the Bretton Woods Agreements," or to explain the terribly complicated system of international exchange, the workings of commodity accounts, or how exchange funds are manipulated for the purposes of earning an income.
How can one explain Canada's present shortage of development capital when Canadians and Canadian companies are investing $5 billion in the United States? Because of this government's restrictive measures, Canadians are investing in other countries. Their investments are welcome in the United States. You can see Canadians investing in New York skyscrapers, in buildings in Dallas, Fort Worth, Denver, Minneapolis-you name the place and you will find Canadian investment there. Our people are not only investing in property; they are investing in the production of goods. Why? The reason is obvious.
We, in Canada, have indulged in self-delusion on an enormous scale for the past couple of decades. We have built up huge social programs, inflated wages, shortened hours, and indulged in plain dodging at all levels of industry, from management to the floor sweeper. Apparently some have not learned that you cannot take more out of the economy than you put into it. Consequently, what do we have in Canada: excessively high unit costs of production, low returns, and Canadian individuals and corporations seeking to invest in the United States. Why are they investing in that country? They do not have to face the hassle of government there as we do here. There the government is not hell bent on hassling business and individuals to provide the economic base with which government can take care of the less fortunate.
Somehow or other, anyone who does something constructive in Canada is immediately fingered as a victim, as one who must be cut back to the level of the lowest common denominator, to the level of sheer mediocrity. That is what we have in Canada. Does that thinking extend to our international relations? It is one of the problems underlying our concept of the International Monetary Fund. These things must be examined in greater detail in committee.
I have nearly used up my time. I do not think I have changed my views greatly in the last ten years about the Bretton Woods Agreement. By and large it has worked well. It was never designed for the protection or enhancement of any one currency or group of currencies. It was designed for the well-being of the currencies of the world. There are pluses and
Bretton Woods Agreements
minuses to the agreement, or, as some would say, to the agreement there is an upside and a downside. I hope the committee will find the time to consider this legislation, althought it has a surplus of other legislation it must consider.
I hope officials will explain to us the workings of the international monetary system because, really, no individual member is qualified to add one cubit, one inch or one centimetre, to use modern parlance, to this bill.
In conclusion, I raise a point on which my party will insist. Bill C-18 is related to Bill C-5, and Bill C-5 is to be considered at the report stage. I have set down an amendment to Bill C-5, and I and my colleagues are adamant. There is no way the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) is going to receive reports from the Auditor General of Canada, to deal with as he sees fit. Those reports are going to be made to parliament, and on that point the Minister of Finance will find us absolutely insistent.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE SUBSCRIPTION TO INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND AND INTERNATIONAL BANK FOR CONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker, for this opportunity to say a few words on Bill C-18.
Canada is about to make an important amendment to the Bretton Woods Agreements so that the contribution of our country could reach 1.357 billion dollars in special drawing rights. That initiative, Mr. Speaker, is certainly commendable because it shows unquestionable concern on the part of this country for the fight against poverty in the world.
Indeed, that amendment will allow an increase in Canada's subscription to the International Monetary Fund and to the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development. However, that is not the purpose of my intervention tonight but rather the merits of the Bretton Woods Agreements. It will be remembered that that international agreement was initially intended to provide for the establishment of privileged trade relations designed to put the economies of war-tried countries back on their feet. That was in 1944. Two drafts were submitted at the Bretton Woods conference at that time, one called the Keynes draft prepared by the world renowned economist, John Maynard Keynes, and the other one by Harry Dexter White, special adviser on monetary issues to the Secretary of the U.S. Treasury. The conference passed, after discussion, the White draft. However, the author of the White draft cast a shadow over the Bretton Woods Agreements because he was later identified as a Soviet agent. So now we have to deplore the fact that the agreements did not bring the results hoped for.
Indeed, they had more of an accounting effect in the international play of the balance of payments than of fulfilling the hopes of socio-economic development they had given rise to at the outset. It is being realized today, Mr. Speaker, that the agreements allowed rather the richer countries to increase their wealth and the poorer countries to increase their poverty. There was a desire to protect European countries from the communist threat. However, we see that several Common Market countries must now face a stronger threat that could reduce the influence of those belonging to the free world.
5910

May 24, 1977
Bretton Woods Agreements
That brings me to say that the Bretton Woods Agreements should perhaps be rethought after 20 years to allow, among other things, a real fight against inflation in all countries. All countries of the free world are complaining about inflation today. And, on the other hand, we see third world countries reducing considerably their borrowing or purchasing power. Money costs more and products have risen in price, so Third World countries are not advantaged.
In fact, we might say that the Bretton Woods Agreements have been more benefit to highly industrialized countries reducing more and more their geographic number while reducing also the number of the beneficiaries of those agreements. Of course, the states benefit from it as their balance of payments becomes positive but their enterprises do too. So, indirectly, multinational corporations are the most privileged.
Mr. Speaker, the danger is that so-called free countries lose some of their freedom because such agreements create the feeling that the freedom, the independence and the power of countries are too intensively related to the survival of their multinational corporations. It is dangerous to think that the failure of an enterprise might someday reduce the value of the national currency at the international level.
If South American countries got together tomorrow and nationalized American companies without any compensation, it would significantly reduce the value of the American dollar. It would be so if some countries refused to supply some American and Canadian processing industries.
The Bretton Woods Agreements did not deal with that issue and only provided for the creation of a monetary fund ensuring the stability of currencies and they also help countries with economic problems. However, we might wonder if those agreements with their lists and their statutes, are not killing very slowly our democratic system by encouraging development through big corporations. The communist countries have always followed the philosophy of Karl Marx who said that in its logic, the capitalist system was going to destroy itself. If you consider the inflationary spiral which benefits of course those who are rich and are not prepared to accept a reduction of their income, and if you consider that richer countries increase their wealth and that poorer countries are unable to recover, we seriously doubt the spirit of those agreements. According to the logic of the capitalist system it might have been better if those agreements had a social dimension paralleled with an economic or monetary dimension. It might have given less importance to the notion of profit and balance of payments which, I think, would have been more advisable.
It should be recalled, however, that our capitalist system is certainly the only one that allows the individual to express his creativeness and organization spirit. But such systems should not be allowed to promote the rising up of state movements in various countries, if there is no other way than state interference to cope with foreign business takeover. We must find a way in which countries will not have to become entirely dependent upon foreign businesses to restore their economy,

thus depriving themselves in a non-independent or sovereign manner from their natural resources. The North-South Conference which is to start new sessions in Paris should bring about new hopes. This co-operative spirit between rich and poor countries did not exist in the original Bretton Woods Agreements. We hear a lot about a new economic order which will finally bring about peace among the people of the world.
I hope we shall be wiser this time and rather than moving in a direction which means 30 extra years of broken promises and expectations, we shall opt for an approach that will enable people to enjoy the benefits derived from our resources without being continuously threatened. The Bretton Woods Agreements have done nothing to solve major economic problems; they were simply the product of professionals and experts who are more interested in balancing international accounts than feeding the world populations. I wish to repeat, Mr. Speaker, that the willingness of this government to increase its contribution is not wrong in itself but the organization referred to should reflect for a while upon its true role and its importance to the promotion of a democratic living system. I suggest that the Bretton Woods Agreements have had more impact on accounting procedures than on social considerations. That was not their purpose but if the agreements had had a social impact, they would not have been too bad after all. Our democratic life style at the international level will probably be improved.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE SUBSCRIPTION TO INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND AND INTERNATIONAL BANK FOR CONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to begin by complimenting the minister on bringing forward Bill C-18 at this time in view of its important subject matter. We know that the intent of the bill is to ratify the IMF amendment to provide for an increased Canadian quota for the IMF and the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development. The purpose of my intervention is to make some comments concerning a passage in the minister's speech this afternoon in which he suggested that all of us ought to remain sensitive to the difficult circumstances developing countries face through higher energy prices and a drop in export earnings.
I want to make some comments of a constructive nature about the ramifications of the Bretton Woods Agreement and the revision of the IMF which has now come about and has led to Bill C-18, but before doing so I have to deal with the comments of the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge (Mr. Saltsman). This afternoon he made some comments which I thought displayed a somewhat myopic view. He spent considerable time responding on behalf of the NDP and trying to drive a wedge between myself and the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) who had replied to the minister on behalf of our party.
The hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge made what I consider to be a rather silly attack when he offered, first of all, a premature judgment on the alleged differences between the hon. member for York-Simcoe and myself. I say that because I
May 2V1977

had not yet spoken when the hon. member attempted to drive his wedge between us. I suppose he did so on the rather spurious ground that the hon. member for York-Simcoe was taking a domestic view of Bill C-18 whereas I would be looking at its international implications.
I suggest to the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge that when the hon. member for York-Simcoe and I are talking about a stronger Canada being necessary in order to fulfil international responsibilities, we are talking about the same thing. The hon. member for York-Simcoe made a very strong attack on the economic performance of the government, an attack which I share. The hon. member was warning against high interest rates, trade imbalances and secrecy of negotiations, and he concluded his speech by saying that he does not want Canada to be bailed out by the IMF in the same way the U.K. has been bailed out.
When I look at the performance of the government, and particularly at the way we signed our name to the London communique which issued from the Downing Street summit a couple of weeks ago, it is a matter of great concern to me that when we espouse rather high flowing concepts about how aid to developing nations ought to be improved through international conferences, we do so without at the same time recognizing that we have been unable to solve unemployment in our own country. That is the point that the hon. member for York-Simcoe was making and the nuances of the point seem to have been missed by the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge.
I find the hon. member's attack rather silly, as mine would be were I to attack the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge for a point that he made toward the conclusion of his speech. He made the rather interesting point that part of the reason why we are not doing well in this country is that people are not responding to the call for harder work. His own leader travels around the country making telling points about how hard it is to get work in this country, and I wonder whether his own leader would agree with that kind of comment. However, I am not going to attack the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge since I recognize that he brings a perspective to Bill C-18 which might be different from that of his own leader and the two of them can work out their own approach. I say only that I think it is very unfortunate that the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge attempts to imply that the Progressive Conservative party is talking out of both sides of its mouth in regard to improved relations with developing countries.
If the hon. member wants to know what our policy is, I can tell him what it is, in a nutshell. Our policy, which is the basis for my remarks tonight and I know is fully shared by the hon. member for York-Simcoe, is that international co-operation is now a prerequisite for peace and stability. The primary purpose of economic growth should be to ensure improvement of conditions for all so as to allow every individual on earth to fulfil the basic right that he has to food, shelter, health care, education and employment. These are the things for which we stand. We believe that it is high time we should stop talking negatively about the problem of the rich-poor gap in the world
Bretton Woods Agreements
and should start talking positively about the structural changes which are coming into play and which will lead to an improvement, in human dignity right around the world.
We share the view offered by the Secretary General of the Commonwealth, Mr. Shridath Ramphal, who pointed out to the sub-committee on international development meeting here in parliament a few weeks ago that the improvement in the living standards of developing countries is not only consistent with, but necessary for, the preservation of high standards of living and continued improvement in the quality of life in the "have" nations. In other words, improving the purchasing power of people in the developing regions will lead to increased markets for goods from the developed countries.
Unlike the NDP, we are not advocating merely redistribution of a static world income; what we are advocating is that the higher incomes sought by the poor through commodity arrangements and better access to rich country markets will signal the potential for significant growth in world economic activity. That is the basis for the realistic policy which our party offers on international development.
It is against that background that I now consider Bill C-18 and return to the comments made by the minister in connection with his deepening sensitivity, and those of other members through ministerial representations at the IMF, about the deep problems of the developing nations which now constitute the great majority of the membership of the IMF. The IMF now has 128 members, of whom more than 100 are classified as developing nations.
In considering Canada's role in the revised IMF agreement, I think Canada has a new opportunity to direct our international efforts toward accelerating the process of what I call structural transformation in developing nations. The need for this structural transformation has been made very clear by the final report of the Commonwealth experts group entitled "Towards a New International Economic Order", which was issued on March 14, 1977. As the House knows, the Commonwealth experts group, including the distinguished Canadian, Mr. L. A. H. Smith, Canadian High Commissioner to Barbados, has been meeting now for two years and has published the third and most definitive of its reports on what needs to be done in order to make some structural progress in improving the self-reliance of developing nations. We must remember the Commonwealth experts' report is of particular significance to this House because of our own role in the Commonwealth and also because the Commonwealth contains 80 per cent of the one billion people who live in the Fourth World, that is, one quarter of humanity-people who live with incomes under $200 a year. The ten Commonwealth experts have emphasized that if present trends continue the balance of payments situation of developing countries will become progressively unmanageable. Even under optimistic assumptions prevailing growth rates will not result in any reduction in the income gap between the developed and the developing countries by the end of this century.
80016-34%

May 24, 1977
Bretton Woods Agreements
I would like to interject here by pointing out the seriousness of the growing gap between the rich and the poor, despite 25 years of foreign aid which is now outmoded in its concept completely. The significance is revealed in the report of the subcommittee on international development. That is the report which was tabled in this Elouse last Thursday. It makes the very telling point that the debt of the developing nations has now increased to $165 billion. That is the total debt of developing nations toward the developed nations. Over a ten year period that is an increase from $35 billion. The situation is getting worse as a result of the increased debt which the developing nations are accumulating. I will speak about the causes of that in a moment.
Structural transformation requires many changes in the relationship of developing and developed countries concerning commodity agreements, transfer of technology, and renewed access to capital, which is the most important, by the developing countries. Structural transformation requires a policy framework within developing countries which encourages high levels of productivity and innovation. It is not enough to talk about the responsibilities of the developed nations to move toward better international arrangements. That would only be a rhetorical exercise, unless those changes are accompanied by internal efforts within the developing nations. These efforts should lead to a widespread commitment to the development effort aimed at the whole of society rather than the privileged few. It is a two-pronged attack on closing the gap that is at the heart of the United Nations' message to the whole international community through the series of forums which are going on presently.
The international community has a primary responsibility to find ways and means of ensuring developing countries get the necessary resources they need from outside for their development. These structural changes will require modifications to existing international arrangements. That is what we have before us tonight. Only in this way can minimum levels be reached in all countries. As the Commonwealth experts insist, this represents a precondition for the achievement of greater stability within the international community and of world peace.
We need to adopt more pragmatic approaches in assessing the developing needs of individual countries. One of the tasks to which industrialized countries have addressed themselves is the alleviation of the foreign exchange constraint in developing countries. I have spoken of the immensity of the problem the developing countries are facing with their international debt now up to $165 billion. We ought to view these problems in positive terms, rather than just negative terms.
We must remember what Mr. Ramphal said to the subcommittee on international development. It is essential for developed countries to take part in improving self-reliance within the developing countries in order to expand the buying power within those countries, thereby providing very large and new markets for the people in the developed countries. Thus, it is very much a self-interest argument we are advancing. We

know a number of steps have already been taken in international forums such as UNCTAD IV and now SEAT, which is coming to a conclusion in a week or so.
Without going through the wide spectrum of measures which are before international forums now, such as commodity agreements and the transfer of technology, I want to concentrate on the field of finance, which is proper under the terms of this bill. Commonwealth experts have said that decisions were taken by the interim committee in Jamaica, the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank, which sought to reconcile the positions of the developed countries on financial questions.
Given a very brief review of what has gone on in the past year or two, it is important for the members of the House to consider Bill C-18. We will note that floating exchange rates have been legitimized, and countries have been given the option to adopt any exchange system they wish. The official price of gold was abolished and the principle of making SDRs the principle reserve asset was accepted. The conditions of access to the IMF compensatory financing facility were liberalized, and the oil facility was discontinued. The trust fund, which is funded from the profits of the sale of one sixth of the Fund's gold and from voluntary subscriptions, is expected to accumulate $1.5 billion over four years and will be used to provide balance of payments support to the poorest countries. That action probably led to the minister's use of the word "sensitivity" in his address this afternoon. Moreover, the quotas in the International Monetary Fund were increased by approximately one third, and marginal changes were agreed to in the voting pattern of the Fund to give a greater voice to oil producing and exporting countries.
The capital of the World Bank was increased by $8.3 billion, and the decision was taken to freeze the bank's growth lending at $5.8 billion and to increase the cost of loans made by the bank. Agreement was reached on the Fifth replenishment of IDA of $7.6 billion which would just maintain the real value of IDA lending over the next three years.
However, there are many areas where decisions and action are still required. One of those areas is the decision which still remains to be taken on the proposal to liberalize the IMF compensatory financing facility in a way which would stabilize, around a growing trend, the real export earnings of developing countries from commodities. That is the heart of my message to the minister tonight. I would ask him to consider the improvements which need to be made in the way the Commonwealth experts have suggested. The existing scheme still restricts drawings under the facility, both in respect of annual amounts as well as in the aggregate, to percentages of a country's quota in the fund.
The international community has not yet addressed itself to the problem of how to deal with the change in the balance of payments needs of developing countries in the new circumstances which the non-oil developing countries face. Moreover, attention has not yet been given to increasing the supply of development finance to these countries on the scale required
May 24, 1977

by the capital investment which they must undertake if they are to satisfy their basic needs in an acceptable period of time.
The Commonwealth experts are critical of the fact that internationalization of control over liquidity creation has not been advanced. I will quote a sentence from their report to indicate the way in which they would like it to move forward. It reads as follows:
Measures to increase the access of the developing countries to the credit facilities of the IMF on a scale, and under conditions which would have regard to their balance of payments needs, and the establishment of a link mechanism between SDRs and development Finance, remain in abeyance.
In other words, consideration is asked for linking SDRs and aid. For a long time we have played around with that concept. As one who studies the developing field, I cannot understand why progress has not been made on the linkage between SDRs and aid. The movement of the IMF in the agreement before us is a step in the right direction. We need the support of industrialized countries to take another step forward.
On the question of debt, decisions still remain to be taken on the adoption of guidelines for a generalized solution to the problem of alleviating the debt burden of the non-oil developing countries.
I would therefore ask the government to give serious consideration to implementing the financial recommendations made by the Commonwealth experts, and particularly to consider the principle of building up the SDRs as the principal reserve asset and one which can be a new instrument in the structural transformation of developing countries. SDR allocations on a link basis rather than the IMF quota basis would require smaller aggregate allocations, since countries with adequate reserves would not need to be provided with additional SDRs. In this way the application of SDRs to developing countries could be enhanced. Improved access to existing fund facilities is only part of the larger package of measures needed for dealing with the problems of disequilibrium in the developing countries. Other measures in that package, the Commonwealth experts note, would include traditional capital flows such as development assistance and private investment, all being required to finance the establishment and fuller utilization of the needed production and infrastructure facilities.
We have had a lot of experience in ways of trying to help developing countries, and when the Commonwealth experts offer us some of the lessons of that experience we ought to listen. The first of these lessons is that as long as developing countries depend predominantly on primary commodity exports the gains from resource transfers will be substantially offset by falling and unstable earnings from commodity exports. Arrangements for the stabilization of primary commodity markets are therefore a necessary condition for realizing the fullest advantage from resource transfers. It is in this spirit the suggestion is made for increasing capitalization flows in the developing countries so as to help them become self-reliant and halt the apparently never-ending cycle of increasing aid which, in the end, only makes the problem worse since
Bretton Woods Agreements
most of the aid which must come from other countries includes a servicing factor which compounds the debt.
I believe we ought to increase the momentum of development beyond the merely holding operation so far achieved. For example, the Commonwealth experts look to structural transformation to finance works on a scale which some find it difficult even to envisage at present. For example, programs to arrest the southward movement of the Sahara Desert in the Sahial area, flood control and protection against typhoons in Bangladesh, rural electrification and the provision of pure water supplies in many areas of the world. The experts believe that this would require both a substantial stepping up of bilateral efforts and further strengthening of multilateral and regional institutions. Of course this means maintaining ODA for the time being and recognizing that, instead of going ahead, the industrialized countries are falling behind in commitments. Developing countries not only need an increase transfer of resources but the assurance of a continuing adequate flow in automatic ways.
I want, for a few moments now, to complement the Findings of the Commonwealth experts by drawing attention to the report of the sub-committee on international development which has now produced its second report-the first was issued last year. This report, which was tabled in the House last Thursday, deals with the debt problem. The debt problem might not sound very interesting, but as we get into it we realize that the debt I spoke about a few minutes ago is a manifestation of the need for structural changes to be put into effect, changes which were never anticipated when Bretton Woods was set up following the Second World War, for one reason because most of the nations which were members of the IMF were not even in existence at that time.
As we consider what the sub-committee has reported-I might add that this report carried the unanimous support of all parties which participated in its preparation-I might say that the debt picture is complicated to the extent that most of the debt is owed by countries which are in the middle to upper range of the Third World, that is, countries which have a growing capacity to repay their debt. The debt is not held in large measure by the least developed countries, the reason being that they do not have credit or reputation to justify creditors extending large amounts of funds to them, certainly not in commercial or private terms.
The debt which the least privileged countries have accumulated comes in large measure from international development assistance. It is certainly no concern of mine that the developing nations have difficulty in paying that debt. 1 think they will repay it eventually though I believe some rescheduling arrangement will have to be made. It is in the interest of the private institutions which hold this debt in the developing world to put pressure on the industrialized countries, probably at CIEC as well as in other international forums, to reschedule the repayment provisions, possibly on a case by case basis so that there will be no defaulting. But, as I say, that is not my principal concern.

May 24, 1977
Bretton Woods Agreements
I am concerned about the way in which the nations of the developing world are piling up debt because they cannot find ways to industrialize their structure or to acquire capital in the manner in which the Bretton Woods Agreement was originally meant to make possible in the case of countries which are very much in the driver's seat in the world. The developing nations need access to capital if they are to achieve any form of self-reliance. There arises, then, a debate between the developed and the developing countries. It began in terms of polarization with demands of a somewhat impossible nature being put forward by the group of 77-it now numbers more than 100 nations. For example, they wanted the cancellation of the whole of the ODA-related debt or its total rescheduling. These were steps which it was totally impossible for the developed nations to accept. The developed nations, for the most part, turned an unsympathetic ear to the message which was coming through, namely, that there would have to be changes which would go far beyond aid.
I believe Canada has shown its good faith by writing off the debt owed by Bangladesh, a country which is perhaps at the lower end of the Fourth World scale. But perhaps we have not felt, because we are not contributing to the horrendous figures of international debt, that it is our responsibility to take any leadership role in finding a solution, it is there that I find government action or, to be more correct, inaction at fault. First of all, it is in Canada's interest to note that, of the total debt picture, $9.8 billion is owed to Canada through commitments made through the Canadian International Development Agency, the Export Development Corporation, as well as private banks, and therefore Canada's involvement in the solution to the debt problem indicates that we ought to be more aggressive. That of course was the finding of the subcommittee on international development. The subcommittee report states:
The government does not look favourably on debt relief in the form of a cancellation of debt, conversion of loans to grants, or waivers of payments.
That may be all very well, but I think it would be better if we, as the subcommittee has noted, supported and promoted the creation of multilateral mechanisms designed wholly or in part to provide balance of payments support for the developing countries, notably those mechanisms connected with IMF.
This brings us to the obligation to take initiatives. I will indicate one or two initiatives which the subcommittee thought it would be useful for the government to take. I think, now that we have Bill C-18 before us, it is certainly the moment to give consideration to these views. The first is as follows:
Canada should press for the establishment of a mechanism and procedures for the multilateral renegotiation of debt which will ensure balanced representation of the legitimate interests and needs of both debtors and creditors.
Canada should advocate an international agreement on a set of flexible guidelines concerning how the mechanism would be activated, the factors which would be investigated and taken into consideration and the broad types of policy measures which might be proposed for the debtors and the creditors.
In other words, this is a specific way in which Canada would press an international forum for a mechanism that would, first
[Mr. Roche.)
of all, deal with debt as it is now constructed and, secondly, lead to a way in which there would be a better allocation of existing capital in the world in the manner that the IMF is beginning to talk about. This will, of course, mean our involvement with an increasing number of multilateral, development oriented institutions, such as the World Bank. As we do that, I hope we will press for an international agreement on a set of flexible guidelines concerning how such mechanisms would be activated and the factors that would be investigated and taken into consideration in each case.
In summary, what we see now-and certainly the subcommittee made this point clearly-is a need for improved and expanded multilateral balance of payments support, specifically in the IMF. While the IMF was not originally concerned with developing countries, as was noted by the subcommittee, access to its facilities was roughly proportionate to the national wealth. Now we know it is changing. In recent years it has paid them increasing attention, for example, through the establishment of the compensatory financing facility and the oil facility, and in discussions of the proposal for an SDR link. What is more, through the route of the subcommittee on international development we came to the same conclusion that the Commonwealth group of experts arrived at, namely, that the time has come to advance the idea of an SDR aid link. The subcommittee said it welcomes these developments and urges the further expansion and liberalization of such facilities.
Before I put the report of the subcommittee aside I must note one of its recommendations because it is of such importance as the House begins to consider not only Bill C-18 but the work of the north-south conference that is bringing together such an array of complex instruments which will have to be brought into play to close the rich-poor gap, instruments such as commodity agreements, trade liberalization, transport technology, and improvements in the IMF.
What the subcommittee states is that there is a very urgent need for some central body to gather and report information on all important aspects of Canada's economic relations with developing countries. Such information would include debt, both public and private, as well as aid, trade, and other relevant statistics.
I find a great amount of difficulty-the minister may not because he has a lot more help than I do-as I try to bring together in my mind the various ways in which our government is responding to the whole development question in the developing world, as we try to reconcile the various policies of the government implemented by aid through CIDA and the spending of $1.1 billion, and the problems it has with trade liberalization and industrial adjustment programs that we are beginning to talk more and more about, and international financing agreements. I think it is in the interests of the government to reconcile those policies, not only with an interdepartmental committee that may be meeting on an ad hoc basis, but in some formal instrument.
That is why I think the time has come for the appointment of an advisory committee on international development to be
May 24, 1977

made up of representatives not only of the House but representatives of business, labour, the academic community, churches, those main bodies in our country, particularly NGOs who have a constructive interest in bringing together the policies of the government, so that if we are at least going to take a pragmatic view, and if we are going to spend $1.1 billion just on CIDA, we should try to have all our policies harmonized so that we could get better value for the money we are giving. Only in this way can parliament and the general public begin to understand the interrelationship of issues, problems, and performance of Canada's response to the UN's call for a new economic order. That is the thrust of the subcommittee's report.
I conclude on that note and ask the minister, when he closes the debate, to give me a response as to whether or not the SDR aid link is a realistic policy which should be given serious consideration at this time inasmuch as serious bodies are bringing it before us. The ultimate goal should be the evolution of IMF into institutions performing functions in the international sphere similar to those of a central bank in a national economy. That is the way the world is going and 1 think it is in Canada's interest to advance in that way.
We need to stress a more balanced participation in the decision making process of the Fund by all groups of countries, including the developing countries. The present serious imbalance between the developing countries in the control and management of international financial institutions is a consequence of transplanting to the sphere of these institutions the principle of voting rights being proportional to financial contribution. I am quoting from the Commonwealth experts' report which states that this principle, which may be appropriate in the corporate sector in an industrial society, is not necessarily valid in relation to the purposes of international institutions. For this reason, the capital structure and voting rights in the regional development banks which were established later are different. We could learn from the original Bretton Woods Agreements. A similar approach needs to be adopted in the case of IBRD and IMF.
That is my approach to Bill C-18. I hope that when we get to committee, some of the details of the bill can be worked out, but I want to rest my case finally as I restate it again, because I want to make clear the thrust of my view that we should consider developing countries should have a priority call on SDRs through some form of linked mechanism. We can see that there are no insurmountable technical difficulties to the establishment of such a link, and its inauguration need not await the completion of a comprehensive package of further reforms in the international monetary system.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE SUBSCRIPTION TO INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND AND INTERNATIONAL BANK FOR CONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to take part in this complex debate this evening on the very esoteric subject of international Finance. I have an historical interest in the debate. In my First term in parliament I resolved at one point never to let an opportunity to debate the
Bretton Woods Agreements
subject of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank to go by without saying something.
I have been moved to study Hansard for December, 1945. That is when the original debate on the Bretton Woods Agreement took place, and I found it very interesting to read some of the speeches which were delivered at that time. There is one conclusion which can be drawn from reading those speeches, and that is that anybody who said anything derogatory about the Bretton Woods Agreement, whether living or dead, has become a minor prophet, because all of the predictions have come true.
Whether there is a direct casual relationship between the predictions and the Bretton Woods Agreement is hard to say, but I can give examples. "In the end it will mean the dissolution of the British Empire." That was said by a former member of parliament for Broadview, not the present member for Broadview by any means, as the hon. member would be quick to point out. Those words were spoken by a Mr. Church. Certainly the British Empire has dissolved, and the prophecy has come true.
Mr. Church said later in that same address that, and I quote, "It will cause dearer money". There is just no doubt about that, as anybody who has tried to borrow from any lending institution lately knows. It was described as "a scheme to put United States gold to work." We can recall that at the end of the Second World War there was great concern about the amount of gold amassed by the United States over the years. That prediction was made by a former member for Lethbridge, Mr. Blackmore, and of course it also came true. What he did not predict at the time was that we would see the United States transferring a great deal of its gold to France, for example, but it certainly has been put to work since the original agreements. Mr. Blackmore also said that the agreement was "a mechanism for binding the moneys of all the nations to the United States dollar," and that certainly came true.
The hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) has spoken at length about the Euro-dollar and the role it played in the years between then and now. He too was a prophet in his time.
Another speaker in that debate, a Mr. Quelch from Acadia, said, "Nations will be forced further and further into a state of unpayable debt". The hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Roche), who preceded me, reminded us of that prediction and how terribly true it was.
Mr. Quelch also said the agreement was "an act of treachery against the British Commonwealth of Nations", which echoed the original statement by Mr. Church. Again one suspects that the Commonwealth of Nations is not now in the shape it was at the time of the original debate.
Forecasts were gloomy, and the results have not in many ways been good, save in allowing a large part of the world to trade more freely and for the standard of living of a great part of the world to rise. One suspects that the stabilization of currencies had something to do with freeing trade, but again

May 24, 1977
Bretton Woods Agreements
we have reached something of a crisis point. I have a feeling that anyone in this debate who is prepared to make a gloomy prophecy could probably find, given 30 years' time, that he would turn out to have been rather prophetic as well.
The setting up of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank was fought by the then Social Credit members in the House. In fact they launched something of a filibuster while denying all the time that that was what they were about, and they held up the passage of the original bill. I was a little disappointed this evening when I was listening to the Social Credit member who preceded me in this debate because the old fire did not seem to be there.
In the statement which was read to us there were actually words of praise for the International Monetary Fund and for its role in present trade. There were some rather optimistic forecasts as well. I should think that if some of the people who spoke in that debate in 1945, wherever they are, were to get word of this, they might be readjusting themselves slightly in their graves.
However, one thing they would all recognize is that in addition to the International Monetary Fund there is now a Special Drawing Right. That was just being considered during my first term in parliament, and in reading the material which was being made available at that time describing the Special Drawing Right I recognized pure Social Credit, and one can find confirmation of that in articles written much later. The Economist of July 6, 1974, for example, talking about the re-evaluation of the Special Drawing Rights, said, and I quote:
When SDRs were first created in January, 1970, as reserve assets, literally out of thin air, a unit of SDRs was given the weight of gold equivalent, at the then official price, to one dollar.
The reference to thin air is true because here we have for the first time money which is created and value which is created out of nothing. The same article from which I quoted goes on to illustrate dramatically the basket in which the value of SDRs is set now. It is made up of U.S. dollars, 40 cents; the South African rand, 0.8 cents; the Austrian schilling, 22 groschen; the Spanish peseta, 1.1 pesetas, the Norwegian krone, 9.9 oere; the Danish krone, 11 oere; the Australian dollar, 1.2 cents; sterling, 4.5 pence; the French franc, 44 centimes; the yen, 26 yen; the Canadian dollar, 7.1 cents is our proportional share; and a few other currencies are listed as well. I always look a little suspiciously at graphs like that. It is described as a basket.
The hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona knows how, when one comes into international terminology, whether it be with regard to aid, to the international fund or whatever, people love to use the word "basket". I always find it amusing and wonder why it is used. I presume it has to do with Little Red Riding Hood and the basket she carried to her granny, because there was an air of innocence about all that and perhaps a bit of solidity too. I suspect that part of the reason for shaping up the SDR with all these currencies involved is to suggest to the public that it is not really made out of literally nothing but is solidly based, which is, I suspect one of the

reasons why it has not been terribly useful in solving the problems of the Third World.
It is still a rather difficult concept to grasp, and various speakers in the debate have mentioned how difficult it is to wrap one's mind around this whole monetary business. I do not claim to be an expert on it. One goes along rather intuitively, guessing and grasping at it and trying to bring it within some kind of scope of reason, but it is not easy.
Writing about the Special Drawing Rights in The Conference Board Record, John Hein puts this proposition:
Suppose someone offered to give you, for free, ten blue $10 bills to put in your savings account alongside your "regular" money ("greenbacks"), provided you agreed to abide by some rules. First, your "bluebacks" could only be used to buy "greenbacks", and then, only when you needed to balance an overdrawn checking account; second, you must be willing to exchange your "greenbacks" for the "bluebacks" of the overdrawn person when you have a surplus in your checking account. Would you take the deal? You would probably answer, "Yes"-if you thought everyone would work together and no one would abuse his privileges.
It seemed to me that might be a sort of handy guide, but even so I agree with the article in the publication World Financial Markets for August, 1975, which states, on page 11:
The IMF SDR is still surrounded by too much mystery and obscurity to gain quick acceptance as an international currency and standard of value.
That is part of the problem that we wrestle with in this debate this evening.
Another area that we have to be concerned about is the Third World debt reaching $165 billion. Six per cent of that is owing to Canada, according to the report already mentioned of the subcommittee on external aid of the Standing Committee on External Affairs. It is a rather disheartening account when we realize that such a vast sum of money is debt owed by the Third World and that a greatly increased proportion of that is owed to private banking interests-51 per cent in 1976 compared to 31 per cent in 1967. This would strongly suggest that the Special Drawing Right has not really been serving its role as fully as it might.
The business section of almost any newspaper reports on the problems that some nations have. The "Report on Business" section of the Globe and Mail of a couple of days ago referred to the staggering oil import bill of Greece which topped $1 billion for the first time last year. Greece is a rather small country which has almost reached its take-off point industrially but has not quite got there yet.
Another newspaper report talked about Egypt's problems and the fact that the International Monetary Fund was pressuring that country to make some basic reforms in the way it spends its money, a good part of which comes from the Arab world.
I find it rather interesting that in that basket I mentioned earlier there is no country from the Arab oil exporting world, and no currency from the communist bloc is there either. As long as there is trade between the communist bloc and the free world it seems to me that the whole business of international trade and aid will continue to be complex.
May 24, 1977

The Egyptians are constantly in trouble because they spend $1 billion on food subsidies. I spent six days in Egypt quite a few years ago and I can well understand why a food subsidy would cost that much now.
One wishes that the International Monetary Fund might move toward easing the tensions in the Middle East whereby a nation like Egypt could spend a little less on defence and a little more on its people. I think this is one avenue that needs to be explored by the International Monetary Fund.
We find the same problems in Nigeria where planning estimates for the next year total $15 billion and the current projected revenue is slightly more than $8 billion. There is going to be an enormous deficit and the situation is not going to improve.
I should like to make a reference to an extraordinary article in The Economist for May. It is entitled "Two Billion People. A Survey of Asia", and comments on what is needed in a good many of the countries of Asia. The author is Norman Macrae, Deputy Editor of The Economist, who visited the area and put together a rather unconventional report, and dared to take some rather unconventional approaches. Some of his words will be startling to a few hon. members. I know the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona would not agree with everything in the article, until we come to the end. If I have time to get around to that he might find we are not that far apart.
I am sorry the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge (Mr. Saltsman) is not here this evening. I listened to him this afternoon with some interest when he spent a great deal of time inquiring about speech writers for the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens). I found that a little strange because as I listened to him there was no doubt about who his speech writer was. It was the hon. member for York-Simcoe because his entire address was given over to taking apart what had been said. The thoughtful discussion and discourse of the hon. member for York-Simcoe supplied all the substance of the somewhat distorted argument of the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge. I found that a little disappointing because one would have expected some original thought and preparation on such an important subject as this. I hope before this debate ends we will have at least one more spokesman from the New Democratic Party because someone must fill the gap and provide some constructive contribution to the debate. There is no point in moralizing endlessly if no thinking has been done on the topic.
The article I referred to is lengthy so I shall only read excerpts. On page 8 the article states the intention of the survey as follows:
It will argue that government-to-government aid from rich to poor countries (which all worthy people in rich countries most especially want to increase, because it makes them feel worthier) should probably be abruptly reduced, because it now sets both politics and investment into tragically the wrong directions.
I realize those are rather strong words, but the more I think about it the more I feel he has a point. He claims that the survey will delineate some of the things that are necessary in order for successful development and industrialization of
Bretton Woods Agreements
undeveloped countries. First of all, he says, establish a rural total employment, then have the introduction of cost-conscious technology, and finally find some way of making big business beloved and getting small government out of its way. Those are ideas that we might all consider as we look at this bill that deals with some hope for the Third World.
At page 17 of the article he offers four steps to take as follows:
Go for total employment in the countryside, at just the moment when unsuccessful poor countries are usually industrialising.
There is sense in that. Next:
Put a lot of money into the hands of rural landlords, at just the moment when "progressive" poor countries are usually expropriating them.
There is no comfort for the socialists in those words, and yet there is some wisdom there. He continues:
Then go through a period of exploiting urban workers (i.e., paying them wages below their marginal productivity), in order to increase industrial profits.
That is heresy for most people these days, but he has a point. Next:
Then, but generally at this late stage only, with annual GNP over about S300 a head, tactfully overthrow the rural squires, by a land reform that transfers agricultural production to entrepreneurial small farmers, but without causing class bitterness.
And then there are two other essential steps to development:
... introduce cost-conscious technology, and make big business beloved and get government out of its way.
The article goes on to elaborate. I commend its reading to hon. members of the House. The author examines several countries in some detail and says that important lessons are to be learned from the Japanese. The Japanese have much to teach the developing world. They can show Third World countries that development in a non-European type of society is possible and that such a society can produce a modern nation. It is clear that Japan has retained its own culture, which is not a copy of the western world. Anyone who thinks it is is making a grave mistake.
The author quotes the directive given by the United States government to General MacArthur, who was put in charge of Japan after the war. The plight of post-war Japan was as desperate as that of any undeveloped nation. The country had been absolutely flattened. The directive issued to General MacArthur said:
You will not assume any responsibility for the economic rehabilitation of Japan or the strengthening of the Japanese economy. You will make clear to the Japanese people that: (a) You will assume no obligations to maintain, or have maintained any particular standard of living in Japan.
The author of the article goes on to say:
This unlovely doctrine of malevolent non-interference helped to spark the fastest advance of any industrial economy in history.
It seems to me there is a lesson to be learned. The author congratulates the Japanese for concentrating on the right approach. They concentrated first on the health of all their people and, second, on their education. We, in this country and the rest of North America, have fallen down sadly in recent

May 24, 1977
Bretton Woods Agreements
years in the way we educate our people. Whereas other countries have maintained an educational system of rigour and vigour, we, following the lead of Dewey and other United States philosophers, softened our education along with that of the United States. That is why we have encouraged so many problems in this nation.
Japan's was probably the first industrial revolution during which, despite large migration to the cities, crime rates went down. We waste much of our natural resources in fighting crime.
The author of the article has some advice for China, as well. He says big enterprises in China should compete with each other. Much of the article will give small comfort to socialists. The author says that it would probably be sensible for Chinese industry, including the towns, but especially industries outside them, to run the sort of welfare services the big Japanese companies run. That would accord with the spirit of the communes. It should be the responsibility of big enterprises to take care of people. I realize that in North America such an attitude would be called paternalism of the worst kind, but it has its merits.
The author considers Korea as well. All these points relate to the bill, to the Bretton Woods Agreements and to the Special Drawing Rights. He says in the article:
The coming economic growth in east Asia, including China's, will not be as export-led as Korea's has been. This will create some balance of payments problems, including for China. I do not think these should be met by govern-ment-to-government aid, which has had all the wrong economic effects (encouraging cost-unconscious technology), the wrong anti-freedom effects (because it increases the power of governments against their people in Third World countries, in each of which it is much more desirable to increase the power of the people against their governments instead), and which would fortunately be regarded as insulting by countries like communist China anyway.
Instead, there should be a return to the original ideas behind SDRs and other devices of the International Monetary Fund. When a country is developing at a good annual rate of growth without excess inflation, then its growth should not be stunted by balance of payments problems. A sufficient number of SDRs should be created-
Note the word "created". I continue:
-to tide it over such deficits. It is unlikely that the excess creation of SDRs would have to be over $30 billion a year. This would add only a fraction of one per cent to the world's internal money supplies and would not be excessively inflationary.
I doubt if that advice will be followed because the Third World owes $165 billion. The money has been lent for a long term, some of it at good, high rates of interest. Lenders will want to collect their interest, and there is the suspicion that there will never be a default. I suspect that we, in this country, and the people of other developing countries will pay the debt in full, if there is not a total collapse. We run the risk of a collapse. If it does come, we will wind up paying for a portion of that $165 billion of debt.
If we continue to run the sorts of deficits which Liberal ministers of finance of the last several administrations have shamelessly run up, we shall find ourselves in a situation where it will be difficult for us to meet the requirements of the bill we are considering. We should know that the difficulties are there to confront us. Let us take note of the sums involved, and

realize that they are separate and apart from the $1 billion which we will spend in direct aid through CIDA. We should study the article alluded to and ask ourselves if we should not separate these funds. If we are contributing funds to the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development, we should ask ourselves if that contribution should not be our commitment. In exchange should we not demand that the International Monetary Fund or the World Bank assume responsibility for those things which Special Drawing Rights were designed to handle? I am thinking of the financing of development in countries which cannot possibly repay money lent under the present system.

Mr. Speaker, on March 8 I drew to the attention of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) the growing aging population of this country and certain research findings which suggest that keeping people working beyond age 65 would be a partial answer to the problem. The minister promised to consider my representations, but I have heard nothing from him.
The number of senior citizens in this country is increasing, and our low birth rate means that this country's work force will be smaller in the years ahead. If present trends continue, in the next 20 years an ever larger proportion of our population will consist of senior citizens. Let me cite the experience of England. It is estimated that 21 per cent of the English
May 24, 1977

population will soon be 75 years old or older. By 1995, 25 per cent of the population will be 85 years old or over. Canada runs about two decades behind the U.K.
In the last century there has been a 30-year increase in lifespan, and the number of retired persons has increased greatly. I point out that the number of people alive today at the age of 65 years represents in total one third of all those who in the past 2,000 years reached that age. This is a great tribute and compliment to science and the medical field.
Today there are almost two and a half million people in England over 75, and in that country's universities there are ten geriatric chairs. Do you know how many there are in the whole of Canada? We have one whole geriatric chair at the University of Western Ontario, from where Your Honour comes. And we had to go to England to get that fellow. We did not have any of our own trained.
More than half the hospital beds today are occupied by old people. This is a great problem. We must do more research to prevent disease so that it will be possible through this research to keep these people in their own homes. There must be geriatric chairs in all universities across Canada, with proper training for those who can be oriented into this field.
Home care should be fully developed to treat these patients adequately and in many cases as well or better as in a hospital bed costing $150 a day. Sometimes people are better off in their own homes.
There should be early diagnosis and care, keeping the patient out of hospital with all its expenses and strange surroundings. This means that the federal government must spend more on preventive medicine which often gets the mouse's share, while spectacular proceedings, surgery and the like, grab the limelight and the money. This is the problem now, getting the money into the field of preventive medicine.
We must remember that the rate of learning varies little with age, as long as you have kept at it. Grandpa may be more keen mentally than you are, even though you may jump higher.
Work hurts nobody. Some people thrive on stress. Churchill, Bernard Shaw, De Gaulle and Ford were at their best and thrived on stress. They lived on it, the stress of accomplishment. People must live. They must have objectives. They must have purpose. They must be useful in this world.
I met a lady in church the other day. She is 101 years old. She went to church in the morning and to church in the afternoon, which is probably more than you and I did. It was a hot day. Afterward I saw her sitting out. She was a real inspiration to everyone; 101 looking hale and hearty. That is the kind of thing we must have, not poor people lingering in their beds in hospital, uncomfortable, suffering over the years, with few people caring or looking after them.
This is why I went after the minister for more care. He said he was going to do something about it. I hope he will because Dennis Timbrell, Minister of Health of the provincial govern-
Adjournment Debate
ment in Toronto took the lead, saying he will have more home care. Therefore, there can be no excuse from the federal government for not going ahead and doing something now.
