speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased that the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Rynard), has spoken further to his concern. It gives me an opportunity to hear the discussion and to reply on a subject in which I am also quite interested. I do so in the absence of the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. McRae).
Where is he?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
speechtext:
As a matter of fact he is not far away. I think he is participating in a pretty exciting event.
The number of people 65 and over will increase significantly. The present absolute number is not expected to double until the first decade of the twenty-first century. The "aged dependency ratio", expressed as the number of people 65 and over per 1,000 people 20 to 64, is expected to increase from 155 to about 190 by the year 2000. In the same period the number of people under 20 per thousand people 20 to 64 is expected to decrease from 665 to about 420. Combining these two figures gives a net decrease in the over-all dependency ratio of from 820 to about 610. Therefore-I think this is a key point-the percentage of people in the working and taxpaying age groups will rise somewhat over the next 25 years rather than fall, as is the popularly held belief.
I want to assure the hon. member that the department is engaged in continuous demographic analysis, including the analysis of future labour force participation of the population 55 years of age and over. There is no doubt that pressures toward general earlier retirement could quite substantially increase the dependency ratios I mentioned earlier, both for the reasons the hon. member for Simcoe North spoke about and also from the point of view of this whole question of retirement pensions. On the other hand, greater flexibility in respect to the present almost mandatory retirement age of 65 could prove to be a very strong counterbalancing force, considering the proven interest of people over 65 to continue part time or full time employment, and considering the likely trend toward tighter labour markets in the future.
I see my time is rapidly drawing to a conclusion, but I want to tell the hon. member that the department is continuing its ongoing study into this matter. I think that on one of the days when we are debating health matters it would be well for either the minister or for his parliamentary secretary to speak on this subject at length, since there is a great deal of material which has been prepared by the department in which I think the hon. member would be very interested.

subtopic: REGIONAL ECONOMIC EXPANSION-MEASURES TO PROVIDE ALTERNATIVE EMPLOYMENT FOR THOSE AFFECTED BY CLOSURE OF LABRADOR LINERBOARD MILL
REGIONAL ECONOMIC EXPANSION-MEASURES TO PROVIDE ALTERNATIVE EMPLOYMENT FOR THOSE AFFECTED BY CLOSURE OF LABRADOR LINERBOARD MILL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure hon. members will not be too surprised at the topic that I am going to raise tonight, not the least of whom will be the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Lumley). I should like to inform the minister, through him, that this is not the last time I am going to raise the matter either. I am going to continue to bring it up until 1 get some realization of the disastrous situation which exists in the western part of Newfoundland, and hopefully I can bring forward a couple of points tonight in addition to those I have previously brought forward.
The minister realizes, as does the House, that some 2,100 jobs are affected, either directly or indirectly, by the proposed closure of the Labrador Linerboard Mill, which is one of the most efficient and modern in existence, built at a cost of $200 million, but which is now going down the drain because of passive interest by levels of government.
I was looking at some statistics, Mr. Speaker, and discovered that besides the 2,100 jobs that are threatened, if we use the multiplier effect referred to by Statistics Canada, there is an effective ratio of three to one. In other words, rather than 2,100 jobs being affected, the true total is over 6,000. If you extend this to the payroll at the Labrador Linerboard Mill, which amounts to $24 million a year, this multiplier effect means that some $70 million is being lost to one part of Canada which cannot afford such a loss, since this is the second disaster which has occurred in the province.
I realize full well, Mr. Speaker, that responsibility for the operation of the mill lies with the provincial government of Newfoundland. But I have to say to the parliamentary secretary, for the attention of his minister, that if this closure becomes a reality in four to six months, the cost to both levels of government in terms of UIC benefits, severance pay and welfare, will be enormous and at least as much as, if not more than, they are going to lose by meeting the losses which occur.
I would also point out that the minister has a responsibility from the point of view of the infrastructure support provided by the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, particularly under the special areas agreements with the province of Newfoundland in the Stephenville special area. I mention a few of these which justify in great part the work done under these agreements, and the programs completed under the agreements, due to the infrastructure support for the establishment of this particular mill.
I will refer to the 1971 figures when the mill was about to begin. There was a loan of $2.2 million by the department to the municipality for water supply. They spent another $213,000 on reconstruction and paving of highways and roads because of the need to provide access from the wood resource. There was the construction of two very large bridges, again to provide access to the wood resource, amounting to $1.2 milfMr. Milne.]
lion. For the influx of population, the students and the children, they built a DREE access school amounting to $1.7 million. That is a total of $5 million under the first agreement. I have no fear in saying that since then another $5 million was spent on harbour facilities and more schools by the Department of Regional Economic Expansion to support the creation of that mill.
The minister must consider the cultural and social effects, as well as the economic impact. I would like to list at random some of those: the relocation of workers and families which will occur; the relocation of businesses, started as a secondary industry as a result of the establishment of the mill; the creation of new businesses, including a massive shopping centre, hotels and apartment complexes with CMHC and other federal funding; the federal government's establishment of an adult training centre; the establishment of four high schools by local entrepreneurship's, provincial government help or by local school boards and local population; the massive undertakings in federal funding of housing programs; the investment in real estate, both private and public; and the commitments made by local municipalities in loans which have to be honoured and will not be honoured because of the economic destruction which will occur.
All this massive funding to support the mill will go down the drain because everybody is only given "pass the buck" interest and passive interest by saying it is not their responsibility. When the axe falls in four to six months, the minister must remember it will be his responsibility, along with the responsibility of the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Cullen), to provide the funding and the administration to help revitalize and rehabilitate that part of Canada.
I can only ask the parliamentary secretary to pass these items along to the minister. Originally back six or seven months ago when I saw the threat, while others did not, that was the time to plan through all the expertise available in the federal government-through the Canada Development Corporation, the Export Development Corporation, the Canadian Commercial Corporation, the Enterprise Development Corporation and CIDA-to find markets, with the aid of the Department of Transport, to support the needs of a four year old mill. This is a brand new mill which is not being given a chance to operate because of bad management and the lack of realization and common sense at the time the political decision was made to put the mill where it is located now. With the expertise available here in Ottawa, the mill can still pay. I hope the minister will take a more active interest in it for the benefit of some people in Canada, thus preventing them from losing faith in what government means.

subtopic: REGIONAL ECONOMIC EXPANSION-MEASURES TO PROVIDE ALTERNATIVE EMPLOYMENT FOR THOSE AFFECTED BY CLOSURE OF LABRADOR LINERBOARD MILL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in response to the hon. member's series of questions on the pending closure of Labrador Linerboard's operations in Stephenville, I would like to place again the role of our department, in so far as the disposition of this matter is concerned, in perspective for this House.
May 24, 1977

The announcement by the government of Newfoundland of its decision to close the operation of the provincial Crown corporation, Labrador Linerboard Limited in Stephenville, is understandably viewed with great disappointment by the people of Stephenville and of Newfoundland generally. That decision was clearly based on the information provided to that government from its experts, including an independent advisory board established in November of 1976 to investigate the viability of the mill. Our department has no reason to question the integrity of that difficult decision. All of the evidence at hand indicates that continuing the mill operation would only increase the level of operating subsidy required, without any real expectation of a turn around in the profitability of the company.
We very much sympathize with the position of the Newfoundland government, which would be faced with substantial continuing deficits if the mill were to continue operations. However, we must emphasize that the mill is owned and operated by a provincial Crown corporation, and it is the prime responsibility of the provincial government. The unavoidable human problems of unemployment and loss of personal income resulting from that decision by the province will, in the short run, be addressed by the application of the full range of manpower and unemployment assistance programs available through the Department of Manpower and Immigration. A joint consultative committee has been established by the province and the Department of Manpower and Immigration to identify alternative employment opportunities and other assistance measures needed for workers displaced by the mill closure. Representatives of the union involved and the community are members of the joint consultative committee.
1 understand that the government of Newfoundland and Labrador is continuing to investigate any realistic alternatives which can be identified to secure the continued operation of the mill on a viable economic basis. 1 can assure the people of Newfoundland that if a means can be found to secure the reasonable likelihood of viability for the mill, in contrast to the very substantial level of operating subsidy presently contributed by the province, we will seek to have all relevant programs of this government immediately directed to the support of the provincial government.
I would like to remind the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe (Mr. Marshall) that the mandate of our department is specifically for the reduction of regional economic disparities through actions to develop the natural opportunities and to build the inherent strengths of each province. We are working toward structural improvements based on the comparative advantage of each region's economy. In the case of Newfoundland, our national programs have been tailored to lead to the greater utilization of that province's resources and the further processing of resource products, diversification of manufacturing and processing activities, and improvements in the efficiency of the business sector. One instrument which the department has adopted to pursue these objectives in Newfoundland is the Canada-Newfoundland General Development Agreement signed in 1974. Since then a total of 13 agreements

have been negotiated with the province under the GDA. I can assure the hon. member-

PUBLIC SERVICE-SUGGESTED COMPENSATION TO THOSE IDENTIFIED AS BEING ON BLACKLIST-ALLEGED ADDITIONS TO THE LIST
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on October 13, 1976, during the question period, the term "extra-parliamentary opposition" was first introduced into the records of the House. The then minister of state for urban affairs was questioned about the existence of a blacklist connected with this term. He asserted that the blacklist charge was very serious. Fortunately though, he added, it was without foundation.
On January 24, 1977, I questioned the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) about the list. He responded by saying, "I have not the slightest idea what the hon. member is talking about." The very next day the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) said he had never heard or seen such a list. The President of the Privy Council (Mr. MacEachen) also pleaded total ignorance. On January 26 the Solicitor General (Mr. Fox) said no such thing existed, nor did it ever exist.
On that day I arranged a meeting in the Opposition Lobby beween the Solicitor General, the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay), and myself. I produced for the Solicitor General's inspection the letter and the list which I had in my possession. I asked the Solicitor General to give me and my colleague an indication within 24 hours, or by noon of the following day, of the way in which the government proposed to deal with the matter. I told him I would prefer to keep the matter confidential in order to protect the mostly unsuspecting and innocent persons named from further harassment. The Solicitor General informed me through his secretary at noon the following day that he would only answer questions which might be raised in the House. That, Mr. Speaker, was the day on which I read the letter into the record , omitting the names from the letter and the list.
Why was I so concerned about this matter? In order to understand this, one must understand the seriousness of the allegations which are contained in the letter identifying 21 persons, as well as an additional three whose names were included in the text of the letter as being members of the New Left.
May I quote a short paragraph from the letter?
The EPO concept, in the context of the New Left, does not mean legitimate pressure group activity but rather the creation of counter or parallel institutions within society but opposed to it and to the electoral process. Through such institutions the New Left seeks to organize and radicalize the "under classes" of society and mold them into a revolutionary force capable of overthrowing the present socio-political system.

May 24, 1977
Adjournment Debate
I quote further:
The radical EPO program of the Left is, in short, a movement strategy predicated on a total and unequivocal rejection of representative democracy, its destruction and the creation of radical alternatives.
Several of the people named in the letter had their public careers rudely interrupted. In the case of Mr. Walter Rudnick-i, dismissal did not take place until several years later. Some people on the list have clearly suffered as a result of being labelled subversives and revolutionaries. One of the more notable examples is Rudnicki who was dismissed from CMHC on what has been demonstrated to be a drummed-up charge. Rudnicki has also documentation to prove that the blacklisting had the effect of cutting him off from access to cabinet documents which he needed to do his work as an executive director of policy planning in CMHC; denying him access to French language training in Quebec City which, after 18 years of public service, he had earned and for which he was eligible; denying him promotion in the new urban ministry, in which he played a leading role in conceptualizing and getting established; prejudicing his relationship with senior staff in the system and with ministers for whom he worked. Most other cases are similar.
My concern tonight is over the fact that the Prime Minister and several of his colleagues still refused today to offer any comfort to any persons on the list which has now been published in several major newspapers in the country. We are asking for the setting up of a tribunal through which these people, if they so desire, could clear their names and lay claim to redress. I consider it incredible that the government should again today stonewall any attempt to gain information with respect to the inquiry which led to the compilation of the list in the first place. Again the government is suppressing the truth. It has been accused of deliberately misleading the House previously, and the charges which are laid here in the House were never answered. The House and Canadians in general deserve a public inquiry now. The sooner the government complies with this request, the less embarrassing it will be for the Prime Minister and his colleagues.
In 1939, Joseph Stalin had something which was called an EPO list, which was the enemy of the people list. In 1970 the
Prime Minister conceived an EPO list, which is the extra-parliamentary opposition. I ask, opposition to what? What is parliament in opposition to? Is it in opposition to the social political system of our country, or is it an opposition to the Trudeau super group that sits across from us? The Canadian people and this House deserve and need some answers.

subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE-SUGGESTED COMPENSATION TO THOSE IDENTIFIED AS BEING ON BLACKLIST-ALLEGED ADDITIONS TO THE LIST
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Prince George-Peace River (Mr. Oberle) has made reference to a letter written almost six years ago by the then solicitor general to certain of his cabinet colleagues which expressed concern that some government employees might deliberately release classified government information without authorization:
The letter read into the record, on January 26, by the hon. member suggested that steps be taken to ensure that these government employees be fully advised and briefed as to their responsibilities for ensuring the security of classified government information.
As the current Solicitor General (Mr. Fox) has stated on more than one occasion, the letter of his predecessor and the names that were appended did not constitute a black list, and the term black list did not originate on this side of the House. Names of the individuals concerned were given to the ministers responsible for the departments and agencies concerned. The letter was written in confidence and was transmitted with the utmost discretion.
Although great care and discretion were exercised in the transmission of the letter to ministers in order that it would not be harmful to the reputations of the individuals involved, not everyone shares the government's concern for the right to privacy of individuals.
The letter was written almost six years ago. Since that time, some of those mentioned have left the government service, others have stayed, indeed have been promoted. Circumstances change, and while there may have been cause for concern in 1971, at the present time the RCMP security service has no interest in any of the persons or organizations mentioned in the letter written by the then solicitor general of the attachment, and this has been so for some years now.
